The Thermostat Was Still Set to Seventy-Two

At a quarter past noon on a Saturday in March 2016, four hours after my father died, I was standing in my parents’ kitchen with a phone in my hand and nobody left to call.

I had made four calls. Dale, who was driving in from a job in Waverly. My brother in Tucson, who said he’d get the first flight he could. Our pastor. The woman who ran the church prayer chain, because Mom asked me to, and because otherwise she’d have heard it from someone else by supper.

The people whose job it is to come had come, done what they do, and gone. Mom was in the front room on the davenport with a neighbor holding her hand. The kitchen hadn’t changed since 1994. Same almond refrigerator, same border of blue geese Mom hung that year and never tired of. By the wall phone sat a pharmacy notepad with Dale’s work number penciled on it in Dad’s square printing, though Dad knew it by heart.

By the back door was the thermostat, a round Honeywell dial with a cracked cover. It was set to seventy-two.

My father turned it up to seventy-two every morning at six, for Mom, and down to sixty-four every night at ten, for the gas bill. He had done that for as long as I could remember. He’d turned it up that morning. Tonight nobody would turn it down unless somebody decided to.

That was the first thing I understood about the next ninety days, though I couldn’t have said it then. It arrives as the funeral beside the bank beside the thermostat, all in the same pile.

I wrote the time on the pharmacy pad. Under it I wrote “thermostat,” crossed it out, and wrote it again.

Dale came in the back door at ten to one. He looked at the dial, then at me.

“Leave that,” he said. “I’ll turn it down tonight.”

The shape of ninety days

I’ve done this for both of my parents. My father’s death was sudden, and nothing was ready. My mother died at home under hospice care in 2019, with most of the decisions made ahead of time, and that was hard in a different way. Between the two, I learned that the shape of these weeks is far more predictable than grief is.

The first week is loud. The phone rings, people drop by with food, the funeral home needs answers, and there’s a service to get through. You will make more decisions in those seven days than in the two months after, most of them on very little sleep.

The second week goes quiet. The family from out of town flies home. The refrigerator is full of dishes you’ll have to return. You may think the worst is over, and in one sense it is.

Then come two months of envelopes. Statements, premium notices, letters with your mother’s or father’s name showing through the little window. Each one wants something: a certified copy, a form, a signature you may or may not have the right to give. Nobody warns you about this part, because by then the people who would have warned you have gone home.

Ordered by the clock

This book follows time, not topic, because time is the one thing you can feel right now.

Chapters 1 and 2 cover the first forty-eight hours: what happens in the first hours after a death, and how to arrange a burial or cremation without being overcharged. Chapters 3, 4 and 5 are week one: certified death certificates, securing the house and everything in it, and who has to be told. Chapters 6 through 9 are weeks two to four, when the will turns up (or doesn’t), the bills start, and there are benefits to check and money nobody mentioned. Chapters 10, 11 and 12 carry you through months two and three, ending on day ninety.

Every chapter opens with a line that tells you where it sits on the calendar, so you can start in the middle.

If the death was today, read the short list at the end of this introduction, then Chapter 1, and stop there. I mean stop. What you’re setting aside is almost the whole book, and none of it is harmed by a night: the prices, the forms, the phone calls, the benefits, the envelopes. Every office you’d want is either shut or about to be. The only things that genuinely move in the next few hours are where your parent’s body goes and whether anyone official still needs to see the room the way it is.

If it was last week, find your day in Chapters 2 through 5 and read the opening page of each chapter you skipped. You’re past the part that can’t be undone, and into the part where small errors cost weeks. Two things in those chapters run on a clock that doesn’t wait for you to feel ready: an empty house in the wrong weather, and a count you make once and pay for twice if you get it wrong. The rest of week one is sequence, not speed. Doing the right thing on Thursday beats doing four wrong things on Monday.

If it was a month ago, start at Chapter 6. The decisions that had an audience are behind you, and what’s left is paper arriving at a house nobody lives in. You’ve probably already done something in this book out of order, and that’s fine; almost nobody gets the first three weeks tidy. Two things are worth going back for. Read Chapter 3 before you order another certified copy of anything. Read the four-pile sort in Chapter 7 before you pay one more bill with your own money.

Each chapter has one tool in it: a checklist, a script, a counting sheet. They’re meant for paper and a pen, at a kitchen table or in a parked car outside a county office.

You may be the executor. You may be the one who lives closest, which often feels like the same job and in law is nothing like it. I’ve written for both of you, and where the difference matters I’ll point it out.

Three early mistakes

I’ve watched families make the same three mistakes in the first weeks, and I made one of them myself.

The first is paying bills that aren’t yours to pay. A bill with your father’s name on it feels like an obligation, and paying it feels like looking after him. According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a person’s debts are generally paid out of the money or property they left, and survivors generally aren’t responsible unless they shared the debt. There are exceptions, and Chapter 7 goes through them one at a time. The default is not your checking account.

Open the envelope. Date it. Don’t pay it yet.

The second is giving things away before anyone has made a list. The neighbor who always borrowed the snowblower asks if he can keep it. A grandson would love the watch. These are kind requests from kind people, and saying yes in week one is how families stop speaking to each other in month three. Chapter 4 has the rule for what stays in the house, and Chapter 11 has a fair way to divide it later.

The third is ordering death certificates by guessing. The funeral director will probably ask how many certified copies you want, and early, before you’ve thought about who needs one. No government agency publishes a right number, and I’m not going to invent one. What you can do is find out which places actually require a certified copy and order to that count. Chapter 3 has the counting sheet, and the story of how I learned this the slow way.

Count, then order.

Where this book stops

This book covers the first ninety days, and it stops at the courthouse door. If you’re the executor and the estate goes through probate, the court side of that job is in The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide. If these weeks have you looking hard at your own papers, that’s Estate Planning for Beginners. I won’t re-teach either one here. Where a subject crosses the line, you’ll get a sentence and a title.

Who’s talking, and when she’ll send you elsewhere

I’m Ruth Calloway. I’m sixty-one. Home is Chillicothe, Ohio, a short drive from the farmhouse where my father turned that dial every morning. For twenty-seven years I did the bookkeeping for Dale’s heating-and-cooling business, which is where I learned to count things before I trust them. I hold no license in law, tax, finance or medicine. What’s here is what I learned doing this for my own parents, checked against official sources.

Those sources are named where they’re used. Most of them are federal: the Social Security Administration, the Federal Trade Commission, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the IRS, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Postal Service and Medicare.gov. One is easy to miss. The CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics keeps the state-by-state index of vital records offices, and you’ll use it in Chapter 3. When I give you a figure, I’ll tell you whose it is and what year it’s from.

A good deal of what happens in the first two weeks is state law, and I’m in Ohio. That is a real limit on this book, and I’d rather state it plainly than paper over it.

Here is the shape of what I can’t answer from here. Who may pronounce a death, and when a coroner or medical examiner has to be involved. Who gets the final say on burial or cremation when the family splits. Whether there’s a waiting period before a cremation. What a certified copy of a death certificate costs, who’s allowed to order one, and how many a county will issue at a time. What the DMV wants in order to cancel a licence or move a title. Whether a bank will open a safe deposit box before an estate is opened. Whether a surviving spouse owes a particular debt at all.

Those are eight different answers in fifty different places, and a book that guesses at them is worse than a book that says it doesn’t know. So each time one comes up, you’ll get the question to ask and the office that owns the answer: the state vital records office, the funeral director or state funeral board, the state DMV, the state insurance department, the county probate clerk. Ask them. Then write the answer down with the date and the name of the person who gave it to you, because in six weeks you won’t remember which one of four people said it, and you will need to.

Get it in writing where you can.

And I’ll tell you when to stop reading and call someone. A collector who says you personally owe the money. A will someone means to fight. A house owned jointly with a mortgage still on it. Grief that has stopped moving and started to look like something a doctor should hear about. In each of those places I’ll name the professional, whether that’s a lawyer, a CPA or a doctor, and say why, at the point where it comes up.

The next six hours

If your mother or father died today and you haven’t slept, this is all you need for now. The rest of the book will keep.

  1. If no nurse, doctor or emergency crew has been there yet, make that call first. If your parent was enrolled in hospice, follow the hospice agency’s own after-death instructions and call its twenty-four-hour number; federal hospice rules require nursing services to be routinely available on a twenty-four-hour basis, seven days a week, so somebody will answer. If there was no hospice, call 911. The National 911 Program’s standing instruction is to dial 911 immediately when you need emergency help. Either way, if the death was sudden, unexpected or involved an injury, say that out loud on the call, and move nothing until someone official tells you that you may.
  2. Call one person who can come and sit with you. Not the person with the most opinions. The one who will sit.
  3. Find paper and a pen. Write down the time of death as you were told it, and the name and phone number of everyone who came to the house or spoke to you at the hospital. Chapter 1 turns this into a proper log.
  4. If you’re asked which funeral home or crematory should take your parent, you may name one for that purpose only. Transport tonight; arrangements tomorrow, in daylight. If your faith calls for a quick burial, say so on that first call.
  5. Lock the doors. Feed whatever needs feeding. Put your parent’s wallet, phone, keys and medications together in one place you’ll remember.
  6. Leave Social Security for another day; the Social Security Administration says funeral homes generally report deaths to it, and Chapter 5 covers what to do if yours doesn’t. Leave the bank for another day too. Pay nothing.
  7. Sign no contracts tonight, and promise nobody anything in the house.

Then lie down, even if you can’t sleep. Somebody else can turn the thermostat down.

Chapter 1: The First Few Hours

The squad was already in the driveway when I got there, a little after half past eight on that Saturday morning in March, backed in over the gravel with the diesel still running and the light bar turning against the side of the barn.

Mom had called them and then called me. Twenty minutes from my house to theirs, and I don’t remember any of the drive.

The storm door was propped open with somebody’s boot. They’d pulled a kitchen chair out into the hallway, the way you do when there isn’t room. A young medic came out to meet me on the step, and he was kind about it, and then he said the thing that I have thought about every year since.

“Do you have a funeral home?”

I said I didn’t know. He nodded and waited, because waiting was all he could do. He wasn’t allowed to pick one for me. He wasn’t allowed to tell me what happened next, either, because what happened next depended on things neither of us had said out loud yet.

That is the first hour. Everyone in the room has a job, every job is narrow, and the space between those jobs is yours.

Which of the three mornings you’re in

There are really only three versions of this, and almost everything about the next few hours follows from which one you got.

The first is an expected death at home, with hospice already involved. If your mother or father was enrolled in hospice, your first call is to that agency’s twenty-four-hour number, and you follow the instructions they gave you when they set up the plan of care. Those instructions are not generic. They were written for your parent, by the team Medicare says you and your family work with to set that plan up, and they usually tell you exactly what to do with medications, who the attending doctor is, and whether a nurse is coming out. Under the federal hospice rules at 42 CFR 418.100, nursing, physician and drug services have to be routinely available twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. So call that number at two in the morning, and follow the instructions the agency gave you, even if the voice on the other end belongs to someone you’ve never spoken to.

If you can’t reach hospice, or you aren’t certain your parent has died, or you think anyone in that house is in danger, call 911 and do what the dispatcher tells you. A squad arriving at a hospice death is not a disaster.

The second version is a death in a hospital or a nursing facility. Here the staff own the first hour and they have done it before. Somebody will come and tell you, somebody else will come and ask you questions, and the two of them may not be in touch with each other. Your job is to slow it down by about ten percent and find out who’s running it. The question is: who is handling this from here, and what do you need from me today.

The third version is mine. Sudden, unattended, at home, with no hospice and no plan. Here you call 911, and you say what you found, in plain words, as early in the call as you can manage. That is what the federal National 911 Program tells people to do, and the dispatcher takes it from there.

If you are not certain the person has died, that is not a question for a book. Call and do exactly what the dispatcher tells you, including starting chest compressions if they tell you to, and let them call it off. Nobody has ever been sorry for that.

Say the hard words on the first call

Whichever version you’re in, there are facts that change what the people coming will do, and you want them said in the first thirty seconds rather than discovered in the hallway.

That the death was sudden, or unexpected, or came after a fall or an injury. That there was alcohol or a new medication involved. That nobody had seen your parent since Thursday. That there’s a do-not-resuscitate order or a POLST form on the refrigerator, in which case go get it and have it in your hand before they come through the door. Whether that document should exist in the first place, and how a family puts one in place, is Estate Planning for Beginners, and I’m not going to use your morning on it.

And then the hard part, which is to stop tidying.

If the death was sudden, move nothing. Not the glass. Not the pill bottles. Not the blanket that is half off. It feels wrong, because your whole body wants to make your mother or father look cared-for before strangers walk in, and I understand that completely. Do it anyway. The people who arrive may need the room as it is, and once you’ve moved something you can’t unmove it.

Move nothing yet.

Who pronounces, and why I can’t tell you

Somebody has to formally determine that the death has occurred and put a time on it. Who is allowed to do that is state law, and it also depends on which of the three mornings you’re in. In one state a hospice nurse may pronounce. In another it’s a physician, or the coroner’s office, or a specific procedure over the telephone. I’m in Ohio, you may not be, and a book that guesses at this is worse than a book that admits the limit.

So don’t guess, and don’t let a relative guess for you. Ask the people standing in front of you. The hospice nurse knows. The facility’s charge nurse knows. The 911 dispatcher and the crew in your driveway know. Ask it flatly:

“Who is pronouncing, and what time are they putting down?”

Then write the answer on whatever paper is nearest, and write whose mouth it came out of. That time of death is going to be asked of you by six different organizations over the next three months, and every one of them will act as if you obviously know it.

The question that tells you how the day will go

There’s a second question, and it’s the one that actually decides your afternoon.

“Is this being released to a funeral home, or is it going to the medical examiner first?”

If the medical examiner or coroner takes jurisdiction, ask where your parent is being taken, whether the office expects to release them to the funeral home, and who will update you. Local law and the facts of the death control the timing. In some cases there’s an examination, and you’ll be told about it rather than asked. This, too, is state law, and the circumstances that trigger it differ from one state line to the next, so ask the question instead of assuming.

It is not a judgment on your family. I’ve watched people hear the word “coroner” and go grey, convinced that somebody thinks they did something. Usually it means the death was sudden, or unattended, or doesn’t yet have a doctor willing to certify a cause. It is paperwork wearing a frightening coat.

What it does mean is that you should not promise anyone a date. Not a service, not a viewing, not a flight home for a cousin. Say “I’ll know more tomorrow,” and mean it.

If you are ever in the small minority of cases where the questions turn from what happened to what you did, stop talking and call a lawyer. That is a rare morning, and it is not one to improvise through.

What a pronouncement gives you, and what it doesn’t

Here’s where a lot of families lose a week, and it’s such a small misunderstanding.

The pronouncement produces a time of death, and that time goes onto a record that other people fill in and sign. It is not a death certificate. Nobody is going to hand you a document at the house. The medic will not have one in the truck. The nurse will not print one.

The certified death certificate comes later, from your state or county vital records office, and the funeral director usually gets the first batch for you. How many you’ll need and how to count them is Chapter 3, and that chapter exists because I got it wrong.

For now, understand only this: for the next several days you may have nothing on paper proving your parent died. You will still be expected to function. That is normal, and it is not a sign that you’ve missed a step.

The only decision you actually have to make today

You’ll be asked where your parent should go. That’s it. That is the single decision the first hours genuinely require, and it is smaller than it feels, because it does not have to be the final one.

What you’re arranging is transport. A vehicle and two people. You are not buying a funeral at nine in the morning in your mother’s hallway, and anyone who tries to sell you one there has told you something useful about themselves.

Say it in these words, or something close:

“I’m not making arrangements today. I’m asking you to transport, and we’ll come in tomorrow to talk about the rest.”

Then ask two questions and write down the answers. What do you charge for the transfer. And if we decide to use a different funeral home, what happens to that charge. The Federal Trade Commission’s Funeral Rule says a funeral director has to give you price information on the telephone when you ask for it, and you don’t have to give your name first. The written documents come at set points later: a General Price List that’s yours to keep when you visit to make arrangements, and an itemized statement of what you’ve chosen after you select and before you pay. Chapter 2 walks through all of it. Have that conversation in daylight, with someone else in the room.

Two exceptions to “tomorrow.” If your faith requires burial within a day, say that on the very first call, to the funeral home and to the hospital or facility at the same time, so nobody is working to the wrong clock. And if your parent had already chosen and paid a funeral home, that’s the one to call, and the folder with the paperwork is probably where they kept the tax returns.

If you have no idea which funeral home, pick the one that will answer the phone and say the sentence above. Transport is reversible. Most of the rest of this book is about things that aren’t.

If someone raises donation

At a hospital, and sometimes at home, a member of staff may ask about organ, eye or tissue donation, and the timing of that question can feel brutal. It’s asked early because the medical window is short, not because anyone is rushing you emotionally.

Two things are worth knowing while you decide. The hospital and the organ procurement organization run the process, not you; you can find your local one through organdonor.gov, which the federal Health Resources and Services Administration operates. And if you think your parent signed up as a donor, don’t argue it from memory.

Ask the organ procurement organization three things. Whether a registration is on record. What legal effect it has in your state. And whether the family is being asked to decide, or only to supply information. Organdonor.gov tells people who sign up to share that decision with family, precisely so the family may be spared from having to make it, so a registration may already have answered the question you think is yours.

Donation is possible only in particular medical circumstances, so if nobody raises it, nothing has gone wrong. If nobody raises it and you have a question, ask the hospital team or the organ procurement organization what decision, if any, the family needs to make.

Have one person in the family speak to the organization, and write the answer down. Then let it go. Families do better when one relative holds that conversation than when five of them relitigate it at midnight.

Three calls, not thirty

Here is the mistake I watch people make at eleven in the morning, with the house still full of strangers: they start calling everybody.

It’s understandable. Saying it out loud is how you start to believe it. But every call you make generates four more, and by two in the afternoon you are hosting a switchboard instead of sitting down.

Call the people who would be genuinely hurt to hear it secondhand, and who need to make travel decisions today. That is usually three or four names. Then hand the phone to somebody else. Pick one person, tell them they are the phone, and let them take the rest. They’ll be glad of a job; most people who turn up want one and don’t know how to ask.

There’s one more category that isn’t about feelings at all. Anyone whose own arrangements collapse because of this death: the aide who was coming at two, the other parent’s day program, the kennel, the neighbor who was expecting your father to drive them to dialysis on Monday. Those calls are short and they are not optional.

Everyone else keeps until tomorrow, and the banks and the government offices keep until next week.

The tool: the phone log

Start this today, on paper, before you think you need it. Mine lives on a legal pad because a legal pad doesn’t need charging and doesn’t lock itself.

Rule one line across the top of the page and make five columns.

  1. Date and time. The actual time, not “morning.”
  2. Who you called, or who called you. The organization, and the number you reached them on.
  3. Who you actually spoke to. First name at minimum. Ask for a last initial and a direct extension, and ask them to repeat it.
  4. What they said. One line. The answer, not the chat.
  5. What they need from you, and by when. The thing you must send, sign or bring, and the date it’s due.

Then add a reference number anywhere one is offered, and date-stamp it.

The rule that makes the log work is a hard one: an unlogged call did not happen. If it isn’t on the pad, you did not make it, and you will make it again in three weeks with a different person who has no record of the first one.

Why bother, on a day like today? Because the first hours produce the facts that every later month depends on, and they’re handed to you by people whose names you will not retain. The medic. The nurse. The person from the facility who said they’d take care of something.

I know, because I didn’t write any of it down. Three weeks later I had the time of my father’s death in two places, and the two didn’t match, and I spent most of a Tuesday afternoon on the telephone finding out which one was right. It was the smallest possible problem and it still ate an afternoon I didn’t have.

Start the log in the first hour. It is the cheapest thing in this book.

Before you lie down

By early afternoon the house will empty out. The squad goes, the nurse goes, the neighbors go home to make something in a dish.

When Dale finally got there that Saturday, he didn’t ask me any questions. He walked the house once, checked the back door, and sat down.

“Did you eat?”

I hadn’t. That turned out to be the thing I most needed someone to notice.

So: the log on the table, the pen on top of it, and the small things gathered into the one spot you named last night. Then stop. Tomorrow is the money day, and you will want to have slept before it.

Chapter 2: Buying a Funeral While You Can Barely Stand Up

Kevin’s flight got in at ten-forty that night, and by eleven he was standing in the kitchen with his coat still on, talking about cremation like it was a line item.

“It’s simpler. It’s cheaper. Dad wouldn’t have wanted a fuss.” He wasn’t wrong about any of those things, necessarily. He was also exhausted, three time zones off his own clock, and trying to solve a feeling by solving a decision.

I had the phone number for the first funeral home already written on the pad from Chapter 1, under the medic’s question. I told Kevin we weren’t deciding tonight. He said we didn’t have forever. I said we had until tomorrow afternoon, and that was true, and it bought us both enough sleep to have the actual conversation like people who loved the same man.

You are shopping while tired, shocked, and short on time

That changes what a price conversation feels like.

Here is the condition the next few days put you in: no time, nothing to compare it to, and no appetite for the conversation at all. You will likely make the biggest discretionary purchase of your year inside a room designed to be calm, quiet, and slightly dim.

That is not an accusation against funeral directors. Most of the ones I’ve dealt with were decent people doing a hard job well. But the condition is real, and a set of federal rules exists because of it.

The Funeral Rule, in plain words

The FTC Funeral Rule, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, exists to let you buy only what you want and pay only for that. You are allowed to pick goods and services separately instead of accepting a package built around items you didn’t ask for.

It has real limits, and knowing them keeps you from being surprised later. It doesn’t apply to third-party sellers — a separate casket or monument dealer you find online or across town. And it doesn’t apply to a cemetery that has no funeral home on its own site. If you end up buying a vault or a headstone from one of those, you’re dealing with ordinary consumer protections, not this specific rule.

What you can actually ask for

According to the FTC’s page on the Funeral Rule, you have the right to:

Price information on the telephone, before you give your name. Ask, and the funeral home has to tell you.

A written, itemized General Price List to keep when an in-person discussion of prices, service type, or specific goods and services begins — wherever that discussion happens, including at your kitchen table or the hospital. It lists everything the home offers and what each thing costs, and it’s yours to keep, not a document you hand back.

A casket price list, in writing, before anyone walks you past the actual caskets.

An outer burial container price list, same rule, before you’re shown the containers.

A written statement, after you’ve chosen and before you pay, showing exactly what you selected and what each item costs.

A written explanation of any cemetery or crematory requirement that forces you to buy a specific good or service.

An alternative container instead of a casket, if you’re choosing cremation. No state or local law anywhere requires a casket for cremation.

The right to supply your own casket or urn, bought elsewhere. The funeral home cannot refuse to use it, cannot charge you a fee for handling it, and cannot require you to be there when it’s delivered.

Arrangements without embalming. There’s a chapter’s worth of mythology built on this one, so it gets its own section below.

That’s a longer list than most people expect, and almost nobody reads it before they need it. Put the list beside the phone before you call the second home.

Three things people are told that aren’t true

“Embalming is required.” It isn’t, as a blanket rule. No state law requires routine embalming for every death, according to the FTC. Some states require embalming or refrigeration if the body won’t be buried or cremated within a certain window; some require neither. Refrigeration is usually an acceptable alternative. If a viewing matters to your family, ask whether a private viewing is possible without embalming, and ask what refrigeration costs instead.

“The cemetery requires a vault or liner by law.” State laws do not require a burial vault or liner anywhere, and a funeral provider may not tell you otherwise. What’s true is narrower and still worth knowing: many cemeteries, as a matter of their own policy, require some kind of outer container so the ground doesn’t eventually sink. That’s the cemetery’s rule, not the state’s, and it has to be disclosed to you in writing and priced before you’re shown any containers.

“This casket will preserve her.” The Funeral Rule prohibits that claim outright, for any casket, at any price. No casket preserves a body indefinitely, metal or wood, gasketed or not, and a seller isn’t allowed to say otherwise.

I mention these three because they’re the ones I heard myself, in one form or another, in the two days after Gene died. None of it was said to cheat us. It was said because it’s what the person saying it had always said. Ask the direct question anyway: “Is that required by law, or is that your policy?”

Reading the bill before you sign it

The bill you’ll be handed has three kinds of lines on it, and they behave differently.

The basic services fee is the one you can’t decline. It covers the things common to every funeral regardless of what else you choose: funeral planning, securing the necessary permits, arranging for copies of the death certificate, preparing notices, sheltering the remains, and coordinating with the cemetery or crematory. You’re going to see this fee on every quote from every home, and you can’t shop it down to zero. You can compare it between homes.

Everything after that is separately priced, and this is where your choices actually live: transporting the remains, embalming or other preparation, use of the building for a viewing or service, a hearse, the casket or container itself, cremation or interment. Decline anything you don’t want. Nobody can bundle it back in.

Cash advance items are things the funeral home buys on your behalf from someone else: flowers, an obituary notice, clergy, musicians. Some homes charge you their own cost for these. Some add a markup on top. The Funeral Rule requires them to disclose in writing if they mark it up, though not the exact amount. It also requires them to tell you about any refund or rebate the outside vendor offers. If a cash advance line looks padded, ask directly whether there’s a markup on it.

What this book will not tell you a funeral costs

I’m not going to give you a number for “what a funeral costs,” and if another book hands you one, ask where it came from. There is no current-year government source that publishes an average price, and the industry figures that do exist aren’t federal data. The FTC’s July 2012 shopping guidance recommends comparing at least two funeral homes; its own cost figures from that page are old enough that I wouldn’t treat them as today’s prices, but the comparison advice holds. You already have the right to ask for prices without giving your name. Use it twice before you use it zero times.

The itemized statement is your proof

After you’ve chosen what you want and before you hand over a card, the funeral home has to give you a written statement showing exactly what you selected and the cost of each item. The FTC requires this timing specifically: after selection, before payment, not folded into a contract you sign on the way in the door.

There’s no required format for this statement. It might be a single page, it might be several, and it will look different from one home to the next. What matters is that every line on it should match something you actually agreed to out loud. If a line appears that nobody discussed, ask about it before you sign, not after. If a cash advance item’s exact cost isn’t known yet, the home is required to give you a written good-faith estimate instead of leaving it blank.

Keep this statement with the phone log from Chapter 1. You’ll want it again when a bank or an insurer asks what the funeral actually cost, and you will not want to be hunting for it in a drawer in June.

Buying yourself twenty-four hours

Back to Kevin, at eleven at night, wanting it settled by breakfast.

What actually worked wasn’t an argument. It was a sentence, and then silence: “We are not deciding tonight. We’re deciding tomorrow afternoon, after we’ve both slept and after I’ve called two places.” He didn’t love it. He didn’t fight it either, because it wasn’t a no. It was a when.

If your sibling is the one pushing for speed, you don’t have to explain hospice rules or grief psychology to slow things down. You need a specific later time, said once, calmly. Then you need to actually call back at that time. The fastest way to lose the delay is to let it drift into three days by accident.

There’s one real exception to taking your time, worth naming so nobody mistakes caution for delay. If your family’s faith requires burial within a day, say so on the very first call, to every party involved, so nobody is quietly working to the wrong clock.

When the family disagrees about who decides

Kevin wanted cremation. I wasn’t sure. Dale had no opinion and wisely stayed out of it. In a different family, that disagreement goes further, and here’s the part I can’t resolve for you from this page: who has the final legal say over burial or cremation when relatives disagree is set by state law. The order of priority among surviving relatives differs from state to state.

Ask the funeral director directly what your state’s order of priority is, and ask for it in writing rather than taking it as a verbal aside. It is not a question that embarrasses anyone to ask.

If the answer is disputed, or the director says someone else has authority to authorize the disposition, pause and call a local estate lawyer before anyone signs. Who can authorize this is state law, and a rushed mistake can be hard to undo. A funeral director is not your lawyer, and the signature on an authorization form is not a draft.

The one sentence about power of attorney, and nowhere else

If your parent had given someone power of attorney to handle money, sign papers or make decisions, that authority ended the moment they died. A power of attorney dies with the person. Whoever held it yesterday holds nothing today, for funeral arrangements or anything else, and anyone telling you otherwise is mistaken. Setting up your own power of attorney, for your own future, belongs to Estate Planning for Beginners, and this is the only place in this book I’ll mention it.

The tool: the telephone price call

Call two funeral homes before you walk into either one. Lead with the questions, not your name. Ask every item below in a flat, unhurried voice, no matter how rushed the person sounds on their end. Write the answer next to each question, and compare the two sheets side by side before you decide anything.

  1. What is your basic services fee, and what does it include?
  2. What is your direct-cremation price, what container and services does it include, and what charges could still be added?
  3. For a burial with your least-expensive casket, what charges are from your home, what does that include, and which cemetery or third-party charges are excluded?
  4. Do you charge a fee to use a casket or urn purchased elsewhere?
  5. Is embalming required for what I’m asking for, or is it your policy?
  6. What do you charge for transport only, if I decide on arrangements tomorrow?
  7. Do you mark up cash advance items like flowers or the obituary, and by roughly how much?
  8. How many certified death certificates does your basic fee cover securing, and what does an additional one cost through you?
  9. What is my state’s order of priority if family members disagree about burial or cremation?

Keep both sheets. You’ll want them again at the actual appointment, not just before it.

Tomorrow we count certified death certificates properly, which is a smaller problem than tonight’s and one I solved the hard way.

Chapter 3: Certified Copies, and How to Count Them

Monday morning, the day after we’d signed the paperwork with the funeral home, I called the pension office with a photocopy of Dad’s death certificate in my hand, feeling official about it. The woman on the other end was polite. She also explained, in the tone of someone who has said this sentence a thousand times, that a photocopy wasn’t going to do anything for either of us. She needed a certified copy issued by the relevant vital records office, not the photocopy in my hand. The issuing office’s certification may be printed, embossed, signed, sealed or otherwise secured; don’t reject or demand a copy based on appearance alone. Not a scan. Not a fax. Not the stapled packet the funeral home had handed me in a manila folder.

I hadn’t known there was a difference. That’s the whole chapter, really, except for the part where I learned it twice.

What a certified copy actually is

A certified copy is a record issued by a government vital records office that the office itself certifies as a true copy of the record on file. A photocopy of one, a scan of one, a PDF you emailed yourself — none of those count, because only the issuing office can create the certified copy. Illinois, for one, draws the line this way on its official death-records page: certified copies are the ones suitable for legal purposes, and uncertified informational copies are not. That’s the entire reason banks and insurers reject photocopies at the counter.

This matters because there’s no master original you photocopy for free once you have it. A certified copy may carry a fee and take time to obtain. Check the issuing office named by the CDC index for its current fee, any fee waivers, the ordering methods it accepts, and its processing estimate.

Where they come from, and it isn’t Washington

Here’s a thing almost nobody gets right on the first try: the federal government does not issue death certificates. There is no national office, no federal form, no 1-800 number in Washington that will mail you one. Death certificates come from the issuing jurisdiction’s vital records office, not a federal certificate office, and that office keeps its own hours, its own fees, and its own rules about who may order a copy.

What the federal government does maintain is a directory, not a certificate office. The federal health-statistics index I mentioned in the introduction, “Where to Write for Vital Records,” names each jurisdiction’s vital records office, how to reach it, and what it requires to process an application. Note that it lists more than states — territories, and in some cases a city registrar separate from the state one, as with New York State and New York City. Chapter 00 pointed you toward this listing in passing; here is where you actually use it. The listing is the map. It is not the certificate. If you remember one sentence from this chapter, make it this one: find the place your parent died on that listing, then deal directly with the issuing office it names.

That listing also means the rules genuinely differ depending on where your parent died, not where you live. Who may legally order a copy is one question. How much a copy costs is another. How many copies the issuing office will issue in one sitting is a third. New York’s own vital records page makes the point plainly: eligibility and fees there depend on who is applying and how they order. None of those three questions has one national answer. Ask every one of them out loud, write the answer down, and don’t assume Ohio’s answer is your state’s answer.

A fourth question belongs in that same phone call and most people forget it: how long the office expects processing to take if you order by mail instead of walking in. Mail processing can differ sharply — as retrieved in 2026, Ohio’s health department posted five business days to process an online order with delivery expected in about three weeks, while Illinois posted roughly twelve weeks for mailed requests. Read the current estimate on the issuing office’s own page before deciding whether to order by mail, online or in person.

Why you probably already have a few

As Chapter 2 noted, a funeral provider may arrange the first copies. Under the FTC’s Funeral Rule, obtaining copies of death certificates sits among the basic services a funeral director performs — but the Rule also treats death certificates as items a provider may pass through as a cash advance. So the provider’s work to obtain copies may be part of basic services, while the certificate charges themselves may appear separately. Check the General Price List and the itemized statement before you assume anything is already paid for.

In practice, this means many families get their first batch of certified copies through the funeral director, who files the paperwork with the issuing office on your behalf. That’s genuinely useful, and it’s also exactly where people like me get into trouble, because the funeral home will ask you, often within the first day or two, how many copies you want. And at that point you have no idea. Neither did I.

The question nobody asks you to answer with a number

Here is what I want to save you from doing, because it’s what I did: guessing a round number and ordering that many. Five sounded responsible. Five was wrong, and not in the direction you’d think.

There is no agency, state or federal, that publishes a correct number of certified copies for settling an estate. Anyone who tells you a specific number — “get twelve,” “get twenty, you’ll need them” — is guessing, the same as I was. The honest approach is slower and less satisfying, but it actually works: you count the institutions, one at a time, before you order anything.

Here’s how that conversation goes. You call the bank, the brokerage, the insurer, whoever’s on your list, and you ask. First: do you require a certified copy of the death certificate, or will something else do? Second, if yes: do you return the certified copy once you’ve recorded what you need from it, or do you keep it? Third, and this is the one I’d have skipped: what format do you accept, must the copy have been issued within a certain period, and may I reuse a returned paper copy with you? Some places accept a certified electronic record and never touch paper. Some want one issued within the last few months. You will not know which kind of institution you’re dealing with until you ask, because it varies by company, not by industry, and sometimes even by branch.

Then count from what they actually told you, in writing where you can get it, rather than from any assumption of mine. If an institution says in so many words that it records the copy and returns it, and that a reused copy is fine, that copy can go to the next name on your list. If it keeps the copy, or insists on a recently issued one, that’s a copy you have to supply. Add a small personal margin on top of that count if you want one for your own files or for a sibling’s, but that margin is a choice, not a requirement from anyone official.

Write every answer down in the phone log from Chapter 1. When the bank says “we photocopy it and give it back,” that line goes in the log with a date, because three weeks from now you will not remember which of eleven institutions said what.

Cause of death, and the one place it matters

Some jurisdictions offer more than one death-record product, or restrict the medical information on certain versions. Ask the issuing office which versions exist where your parent died, and ask the recipient which one it requires. One recipient worth asking early is the VA, if you’re filing for burial benefits. Chapter 8 covers that claim in full; the short version here is that VA says you may need a death certificate that includes the cause of death for burial and transportation benefits. If your parent was a veteran, raise that when you order, rather than discovering the gap while you’re already filling out the form.

Beyond that one case, ask each institution which version it wants before you order a stack of the wrong kind. It’s a sentence added to the same phone call you were already making. Nobody minds the extra question. The clerk at the county office has heard it a hundred times, and the person at the bank would rather tell you now than reject your mailed-in packet three weeks from now and make you start over.

Sometimes an out-of-state office or an older relative insists the certification should look a particular way. Don’t argue it from the sofa. Ask the issuing office what forms of certification it produces, ask the recipient what it accepts, and let those two answers settle it. It’s one more line on calls you’re making anyway.

What it cost us, in driving, not dollars

The second time I drove to the county health department, it was raining, the kind of flat gray April rain that doesn’t let up long enough to make running from the car worth it. I’d ordered five certified copies the first week, confident that was plenty, because five had felt like a generous number compared to the one I actually needed that first day.

It wasn’t enough. The brokerage kept its copy. The life insurer kept its copy. The title company handling the house kept its copy. By the third week I was down to one, with two institutions still on the list, and a fourth that called back to say the copy I’d sent hadn’t scanned clearly and they needed a fresh one.

So I drove back. I stood in the same line, filled out the same form, paid the same fee again, and drove home with two more certified copies that I’d have already had if I’d asked the “does it get returned” question before I ordered the first batch. The actual cost wasn’t large. The cost was an afternoon in April rain that I didn’t have to spend, on top of a month that had already taken most of my afternoons.

If you take one practical thing from this chapter, let it be this: count before you order, not after you run out.

What to do with them once you have them

Certified copies are small, official, and easy to lose track of in a house that’s already full of paper. One labeled envelope, kept beside the phone log and the funeral home’s itemized statement from Chapter 2. One list taped to the inside flap, every certified copy numbered, with a line for who has it and the date it left the envelope. When a copy comes back from an institution that returns it, it goes back in the envelope and gets crossed off the “out” column, not thrown loose in a drawer.

This sounds like overkill for a handful of pieces of paper. It isn’t. The list tells you where each copy is when the next institution asks for one.

The short, flat warning you’ll want to ignore

Ordering more later means going back to the issuing office, likely another fee, and another wait while nothing else on your list moves forward. It is not a catastrophe. It is also not free, in time or in patience, and both of those are already in short supply this month. Count first. Order once if you can. Order again without guilt if you can’t — just don’t guess twice.

The tool: the certificate count

Make one line for every bank, brokerage, insurer, pension office, employer, title company, land registry and benefits office on your notification list. For each one, write:

Does this institution require a certified copy, or will another form of proof work? Does it return the copy once it’s recorded what it needs, or keep it? Paper or electronic? Any limit on how old the copy may be? Will it take one that another institution already handled? Which version does it want, if the issuing office offers more than one?

Total the copies you’ll have to supply because the institution said it keeps them or won’t take a reused one. Everything the institution told you it returns and will accept secondhand can travel down your list. Add a small personal margin at the end if you want copies for your own records or for a sibling, and write that number in separately so you can see at a glance what was necessity and what was choice.

Keep this sheet in the same envelope as the certificates themselves. Tomorrow the work moves to the house — the locks, the mail, the dog nobody’s fed yet — and you won’t want to be hunting for a counting sheet in a different pile.

Chapter 4: The House, the Car, the Dog and the Mail

Marlene came across the road last spring with a coffee cake and one question. How long can a house sit empty, she wanted to know, before something happens to it?

The honest answer is less comforting than a number. Cold weather can turn one unattended night into damage, but an empty house needs attention this week in any season. Leaks, heat, animals and the simple fact that nobody is looking don’t wait for February.

You’re somewhere in the first week now, and the house is the part of this that will not wait for you to feel ready. Paperwork sits still. A furnace doesn’t.

I learned that in the wrong order. When Dad died the farmhouse wasn’t empty, because Mom was still in it, and I spent that week worrying about banks instead of pipes. Three years later, after Mom died, I stood in that same kitchen on the fifth day with my coat on, looking at a thermostat somebody had turned down to fifty in a hurry, and I understood that this was now a building nobody lived in. That’s a different thing to own. A building nobody lives in has no one to notice the smell of gas, the drip under the sink, the back door that didn’t catch.

Dale said one sentence about it, which is his habit. “Set it to fifty-five and leave it. Cheaper than a plumber.”

Heat, water, and the two numbers you write on the pad

Walk in and deal with the mechanical house before you touch a single piece of paper.

Find the thermostat and set it somewhere that will keep the pipes from freezing in your climate, then write the number you set it to on the phone log from Chapter 1, with the date. You are going to be asked by a sibling, an insurance agent and possibly a real estate agent what the house is sitting at, and you will not remember.

Find the main water shutoff and know where it is even if you don’t close it. Whether you shut the water off depends on whether anything in that house needs it. A furnace with a humidifier, a sump pump, a basement with any history of water at all — those change the answer. If the house has a sump pump, the power stays on, and that is not negotiable.

Find the panel. Find the gas meter. If you smell gas, leave and call the utility from outside, and don’t go back in to check the stove.

Write both numbers down. Thermostat and water.

Call the insurer before you call anyone else

Here’s the one I’d put at the top of the week if I could only save you from a single mistake in this chapter.

Call whoever insures that house and tell them, in plain words, that the policyholder has died and nobody is living there. Then ask three things and write the answers down: what does the policy require of you now, what does it stop covering once the house is unoccupied, and what do you have to do to keep it in force. Ask for the answer in writing or in an email you can keep.

I’m not going to tell you what your policy says, because I haven’t read it and policies differ. What I will tell you is that an empty house and a lived-in house are not the same risk to the company carrying it. The time to find out how yours treats the difference is this week, while the premium is paid and the coverage is intact. Not in six weeks, with water in the basement and a claim to argue about.

Ask for it in writing.

While you have them on the phone: ask what happens to the policy itself. There’s a dead person’s name on it, and someone has to tell you whose job it is to keep paying it and from what account. You may not like the answer. Get it anyway.

Count the keys

I thought I knew who had a key to my parents’ house. I counted four. By that Friday I knew about seven.

There was one in a magnetic box under the back step, which I’d known about since I was fourteen and had forgotten entirely. There was one with the man who rented the hay ground behind the house, who had held it for eleven years in case a pipe let go while they were in Florida. There was one with the woman who had cleaned every other Friday, who called me about it herself, which was decent of her. There was a lockbox hanging on the rail by the back door from the equipment deliveries, and the code was written on a piece of masking tape inside the cupboard, which rather defeats a lockbox.

So the exercise is this: write down every person who might have a key, and then call them. Not to accuse anybody. Just to know. Neighbors, cleaners, aides, grandchildren, the church friend who watered plants, the lawn service, the person who fed the cat the last time anybody went anywhere.

Then decide whether to change the locks, knowing the real number instead of the number you assumed. Sometimes the answer is no — a trusted neighbor with a key is worth more than a new deadbolt, especially if you live an hour away. Sometimes the answer is obviously yes. The point isn’t which you choose. The point is that you choose it on purpose, with a list in front of you, rather than finding out in March that seven people could walk in.

Nothing leaves the house

Now the uncomfortable part, and I’m going to be flat about it because softening it has never helped anybody.

Nothing leaves that house. Not the rifle in the hall closet. Not the ring your mother told you in 2011 was yours. Not the tools your brother has been borrowing for a decade. Not the casserole dish that belongs to the neighbor, honestly, until somebody has written down that it belongs to the neighbor.

This is not about mistrust, although sometimes it is. It’s that a house full of a dead person’s belongings is the single easiest thing in the next ninety days to make unfixable. Once an object is gone, there is no list you can make that puts it back, and there is no conversation about who should have had it that doesn’t start with an accusation. A fair way to divide what’s in that house is Chapter 11’s job, and it is a real job that deserves its own chapter. Week one is not the time, and a hallway is not the place.

What you do instead costs nothing: you take photographs. Every room, every drawer you open anyway, every surface. Your phone date-stamps them for you. If a cousin arrives on Saturday and leaves with a clock, you’ll know, and knowing is most of the battle.

If there are firearms in the house, secure them in place against unauthorized access, and leave them there. Who may take possession of a dead person’s gun, and how it may be transferred, is governed by both federal and state law, and I am not qualified to tell you how either applies to you. So before any firearm changes hands, ask a local estate lawyer and a federally licensed dealer what estate authority and what federal and state law require. And don’t let a well-meaning relative drive off with a shotgun in the truck bed because it seemed tidier.

Medications are the other thing to deal with on sight. Get them out of the open, especially anything controlled. If your parent was on hospice, the instructions that agency gave you covered this — go look at them again. If not, ask the pharmacy that filled them what to do with what’s left, rather than flushing it or handing it to a relative who takes the same drug.

The car, and the one place I’d leave well alone

Do not cancel the auto policy. Notify the insurer of the death now and ask, in writing, what must change to keep the parked vehicle covered and who may drive it. A dead person’s name on a policy raises the same questions the house policy raised, and the answers come from the insurer, not from me. Cancelling instead is the sort of thing that feels responsible at the time and costs money later. Get the car off the street and into the garage or the driveway if you can.

Then leave the title alone.

Transferring a vehicle title out of a dead person’s name, and cancelling a driver’s license, are state procedures run by your state’s motor vehicle agency. They differ enough that I’d be doing you harm by describing Ohio’s and letting you assume it’s yours. Look up your own state’s motor vehicle website, find its page for a deceased owner, and read what it actually requires. Some states have a short-form process for a surviving spouse. Some want court paperwork first. You cannot know which yours is without looking, and the cost of guessing is a wasted morning in a license bureau with a numbered ticket in your hand.

Write the plate number, the VIN and the insurer’s phone number on the pad while you’re standing there looking at the car. Then close the garage.

The dog nobody has thought about

Somewhere around day two there’s an animal in this story, and because nobody put it on a list, it becomes an emergency at nine o’clock at night.

Here’s the whole plan, and it’s short. Call the animal’s own veterinarian, because they have the records, they know what it’s on, and they will often board it or know who does. Look for anything your parent wrote down about the animal, because people who worry about their pets frequently did write something, and it’s usually in the same drawer as the pet’s paperwork. Name one family member who has the animal, by name, out loud, so that three people don’t each assume somebody else is feeding it. If no family member can take it, call the local humane society or animal shelter and ask what they can do — not as a last resort you should feel bad about, as a phone call.

Then write down who has the animal and who is paying for its food and its vet. That last part prevents a specific small resentment that otherwise grows all summer.

The mail is where the next three months are hiding

Half of what you will need to know in the next ninety days is going to arrive at that mailbox, addressed to a dead person, from companies you have never heard of. Which also means that mailbox is now the least secure thing on the property, and it’s standing at the end of the driveway.

Start with what you’re actually allowed to do, because this is the place where well-meaning families get themselves into trouble.

The Postal Service draws the line at whether you shared the address. If you lived with the person who died and you keep getting their mail, USPS says on its page about mail addressed to the deceased that you may open and manage it as needed. You may also forward all of it. And you may forward a single piece, to an appointed executor say, without going anywhere: neatly cross out your address, print “Forward to” and the new address on the front, and leave it for your carrier or drop it in a collection box.

If you did not share the address, the rule is stricter than almost anyone expects. To have a dead person’s mail forwarded to a different address, USPS says you have to go in person to a Post Office location with documented proof that you are the appointed executor or administrator authorized to manage that mail. The page says plainly that simply having their death certificate is not enough. I checked it again in 2026 and it still reads that way.

Read that twice, because it reorders your week. Appointment comes from a court, and the court side of becoming an appointed representative is The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide, not this book. What matters here is what you do in the meantime, which is not nothing:

If you shared the address, follow USPS’s shared-address options above. If you did not, a house or mailbox key does not prove authority to manage the mail. Before appointment, call the local Post Office, explain the death, and ask what it permits while the estate waits for papers; contact urgent senders directly. Do not remove, open, redirect, hold, or ask a neighbor to collect the mail unless USPS or a lawyer confirms that you may.

And do not tell the Post Office, or a bank, or anybody else that you are the executor if no court has said so. That sentence is the one that turns a grieving daughter into a person who made a false statement, and it is entirely avoidable.

When somebody does have the appointment papers and files that change of address, know what you’re buying. For a permanent change of address, USPS generally forwards First-Class Mail for twelve months, but periodicals for sixty days; USPS Marketing Mail generally is not forwarded. Mark day sixty on the calendar, because the statements and notices that arrive as periodicals stop coming to you long before the rest of it does.

Separately, USPS’s forwarding page, as it read in 2026, says standard forwarding can be extended for six, twelve or eighteen more months, with eighteen the maximum and the extension non-refundable. Check that page for which classes an extension covers. They are not the same as the standard list. Forwarding may begin within three business days, but the page tells you to allow up to two weeks. When the forwarding period ends, USPS returns mail to the sender for six months.

And the line on that page I’d tape to the wall: a change of address only changes the address with the Post Office. You still have to tell every agency and every company yourself. Forwarding is a net, not a notification. Who you tell, and in what order, is the next chapter.

One more thing on the mail, worth doing early because it works slowly. The Data & Marketing Association keeps a Deceased Do Not Contact List, and USPS links to it from that same page. Registration carries a processing fee — six dollars when I looked in 2026. Register the name there and USPS says advertising mail should decrease within three months of registering. Three months is a long time to wait for a small mercy, which is exactly why you do it in week one rather than in August when the catalogs have finally made you angry.

Reading that mail as a search for money your parent never mentioned is its own skill, and it has a chapter of its own later. For now you’re only keeping it safe and keeping it in one pile.

Do not cancel the power

Last, the trap, because it catches careful people. The careful instinct in week one is to stop the outgoing money, and the most visible outgoing money is utilities.

Leave the electricity, the gas, the water and the internet connected. A house with no power has no sump pump, no furnace, no security system and no working smoke alarm after the batteries go. An unheated house in January costs more in one burst pipe than a winter of gas bills. The internet is often carrying the alarm panel, the camera at the back door and the thermostat you can check from your kitchen eighty miles away.

The subscriptions and the autopay on things nobody needs are a real problem, and Chapter 7 sorts those with a test you can apply to an envelope. Utilities on an empty house are not in that category. If money is the reason you’re thinking about it, call the utility, say the account holder has died, ask whether the account can stay on and what they need from you, and write down who you spoke to.

The tool: the empty-house walkthrough

Do this once, with your phone, in one careful pass, before anybody tidies anything.

  1. Thermostat: photograph it, set it, write the number and the date on the phone log.
  2. Water: find the main shutoff, photograph it, decide on or off and write down which, and check under every sink and behind the washer for anything already dripping.
  3. Power and gas: find the panel and the meter, photograph both, confirm nothing is scheduled to be shut off.
  4. Every room, in order, one photograph from the doorway and one of any surface with things on it. Don’t stage. Don’t straighten.
  5. Keys: list every person who might have one, with a phone number beside each name.
  6. Firearms: locate, secure in place, photograph where they are, and leave them there until a lawyer and a licensed dealer tell you what federal and state law require.
  7. Medications: gather, get them out of the open, note anything controlled.
  8. Mail: if you shared the address, start the one stack that everything joins from now on. If you didn’t, call the local Post Office and ask what you may do while the estate waits for papers.
  9. Perishables: refrigerator, freezer, the fruit bowl, the bag of dog food that mice will find.
  10. The animal: who has it tonight, who has it next week, who is paying.
  11. The outside: hose bibs, the spare key under the step, whether the garage door opener in the car still works from the road.

Then lock it, photograph the locked door with the date on it, and leave.

When this stops being your decision

One honest limit, and it belongs here rather than three chapters from now.

If that house has a mortgage on it, or a second name on the deed, or a reverse mortgage, or a tenant in it, you have moved past what a walkthrough and a thermostat can fix. Call a local estate lawyer this week and spend an hour of their time. I know what an hour costs. I also know what it costs to find out in month four that someone was supposed to be told something in month one, and that the person who was supposed to tell them was you.

The same goes if anyone asks you to sign something about that house — a listing, a deed, an insurance change — and you are not the appointed representative. Don’t sign it. Ask the lawyer whether you have the authority to sign it at all. A signature on a house is not a draft.

Tomorrow the work moves to the telephone, and to the forty organizations that each think they’re the only call you have to make today. There’s an order to that, and it isn’t alphabetical.

Lock the box first.

Chapter 5: Who Has to Be Told, and in What Order

By the Friday of that first week I had forty-one organizations written on the yellow legal pad, in three different pens, in no order whatsoever. Two banks. A credit union nobody had mentioned until Thursday. The pension. A seed company. The gas utility. A magazine about model trains that Gene had let run on autorenewal since the Clinton administration.

Forty-one calls is not a day’s work. It is three weeks of hold music, and it was also the wrong way to look at the problem, because a list with no order in it is just a way of feeling behind forty-one separate times.

Dale looked at the pad over my shoulder and said, “Which of those is costing money right now?”

Four of them were. I did those four and let the rest sit until the following week, and nothing bad happened. That is most of what this chapter is.

Put the money ones first

Here is the sorting rule, and it is the only one you need.

Tell first the organizations where money is moving. Money going out of an account that nobody is watching. Money going in, to a person who is no longer there to receive it. Money that stops the moment somebody learns of the death, and money that keeps coming until somebody tells them.

Everything else waits. The gym waits. The magazine waits. The loyalty card at the grocery store waits forever, and if it never gets told, the sky stays up.

There is a second reason for the order, and it is about your own stamina. The calls get easier. The first one is the worst phone call you will make that week, and if you spend it on a subscription line in a different time zone, you have wasted it. Spend it where it counts.

Social Security, which you probably do not have to call

Start here, because it is the shortest item on the list and almost everyone assumes it is the longest.

The Social Security Administration’s own page on what to do when someone dies says that funeral homes generally tell them when someone dies, so you do not typically need to report a death yourself. That sentence saves most families a phone call. It does not save you the two minutes it takes to confirm it happened.

So do this instead of calling: when you are next in contact with the funeral director, ask whether they reported the death to Social Security, and on what date. Write the answer and the date in the phone log. If they did, you are finished with this item.

If a funeral home is not involved, or nobody will confirm it was reported, then you call. The SSA’s number is 1-800-772-1213, and the TTY number is 1-800-325-0778, available in most US time zones Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. Have four things in front of you before you dial: the name, the Social Security number, the date of birth and the date of death. That is what SSA’s page says it wants. It is a short call when you have all four, and an awful one when you are hunting for the middle item while a recording thanks you for your patience.

If you are outside the United States, SSA directs you to a Federal Benefits Unit or to its International Call Center at +1-855-522-6936. If the person who died was a US citizen, SSA also says to report the death to the nearest US embassy or consulate.

What you may be able to claim from Social Security is a separate and much bigger subject, and it is Chapter 8. This call is only the telling.

The payment that lands in the account afterward

Now the mistake that costs families real money in the first month, and it is not a dramatic one. It looks like good news.

A benefit payment arrives after the death. Sometimes two. The account is open, the direct deposit is automatic, and the money sits there looking like it belongs to somebody.

Do not spend it. Do not move it to your own account “to keep it safe,” and do not let a sibling pay the funeral home out of it because the timing seems tidy.

I am not going to tell you whether that payment is owed back. The answer turns on the month it covers and on facts about your parent’s record that I do not have, and I could not find it stated plainly on SSA’s own site when I looked in 2026. So the instruction is narrower and safer than the one you want: call 1-800-772-1213, say what arrived and on what date, and ask whether any of it has to be returned and how. Ask for the answer in writing, or at minimum write down who told you, when, and the reference number they give you.

Then leave the money alone until you have that answer.

Leave it where it is.

Medicare, and the thing I will not make up

Medicare gets asked about constantly in that first week, and the honest answer is thinner than people want.

Social Security is generally the agency that learns of a death first, and the Medicare record follows from that record. That much is reasonable to say. What I could not confirm on Medicare’s own pages when I checked in 2026 was the rest of it: exactly when coverage ends, whether a premium gets refunded, how a particular Medicare Advantage or Part D plan is closed out. Those answers vary by plan, and your cousin who went through this in another state in 2019 does not have them either.

So if there is an Advantage plan or a Part D drug plan, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) and ask what that specific plan needs from you and who has to provide it. Write the answer in the log with the date, because you will be asked by someone in your family who is certain they already know.

The employer, where four things sit in one drawer

If your parent was working, or had retired from somewhere with a pension, the employer or former employer is the single highest-yield phone call in this chapter. Ask separately whether there is a final paycheck, payable unused leave, group life coverage, or a pension or retirement-plan benefit. Do not assume any one exists.

Call the human resources or benefits department, say the employee has died, and ask each of the four as a separate question. Not “what happens now.” People answer “what happens now” with the one thing in front of them on the screen.

Ask who the plan administrator is, ask for that administrator’s direct number, and ask what form each item needs. Write all of it down.

This is also where the small forgotten policies surface, and the hunt for the ones nobody knew about is Chapter 9’s job.

Notify is not the same as close

Banks, credit unions and brokerages come next, and there is one sentence here that will keep you out of trouble.

Say, “I am notifying you of a death.” Then stop talking.

Do not say you are the executor unless a court has appointed you and you can prove it. Do not ask them to close anything. Do not ask them to move anything. Do not let a helpful person on the phone walk you into authorizing something, and do not sign a form that arrives in the mail three days later without reading what it says you are.

Who may close an account, move money, or write a check after a death depends on the account agreement, how the account is titled, any beneficiary designation, and the authority the institution requires. Do not move money or close anything based only on this book. If the institution says it needs court papers, the process for getting them is in The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

When you notify the institution, ask what recording the death changes, when the change takes effect, and which pending deposits or payments may be rejected. Have the appointed representative or estate lawyer confirm how necessary property expenses will continue.

Ask each institution the script below, and nothing beyond it. The certified-copy question in it is the one from Chapter 3’s counting sheet, and this is exactly the week it earns its keep.

Insurers, and the policy on the credit card

Life, health, auto and homeowner’s insurers all need telling. The house and car policies you have already dealt with if you worked through the walkthrough in Chapter 4, and the written answers you got there go in the same place as everything else.

Life insurance is different, because telling the insurer is the start of a claim rather than the end of an obligation, and the money usually belongs to a named beneficiary rather than to the estate. The claim itself is Chapter 9.

Then the one people miss. Look at the credit card statements for an accidental death rider, a small term policy sold through a bank, or a benefit attached to a union membership or a professional association. Check statements and membership materials for an accidental-death rider or separate policy. If you find one, call the named insurer and ask what its current claim process requires. The way you find them is by reading the mail and the statements, which is why the pile from Chapter 4 matters.

What can genuinely wait

Subscriptions. Streaming services. The gym. The warehouse club. The magazine about model trains. The frequent flyer account. The newspaper, unless it is piling up on the porch and telling the street that nobody lives there, in which case it is a security problem and goes to the top.

None of those is urgent, and all of them will take a cheerful customer service representative twenty minutes each. Which ones to stop and which to keep paying, and the test for an envelope you are not sure about, is Chapter 7.

The call that took eleven minutes, and the one that took three weeks

Two calls from that first week after Gene died, same morning, same legal pad.

The pension office took eleven minutes. I had his Social Security number, his dates, and an old pay stub with an employee number on it that I had found in a shoebox. The woman gave me her first name and a four-digit extension, told me which form would come and roughly when, and read me a reference number twice because I asked her to. I wrote all of it down. When the form came eight days later, it came exactly as described.

The bank took three weeks. I called their main number, spoke to someone perfectly pleasant, told them Gene had died, and hung up feeling like I had accomplished something. I did not get a name. I did not get a reference number. I did not write down the time.

Three weeks later, when it mattered, there was no record that I had called at all, and I had nothing to argue with. So I made the call again, properly this time, and lost the three weeks.

The difference between those two calls was not the institution. It was what I wrote down while I was talking.

The tool: four sentences and a number

Every one of these calls is the same call. Say these four things, in this order, and then do one thing at the end.

  1. “I am calling to notify you of a death.” The name, the date of death.
  2. “I am the son or daughter. I am not telling you I have legal authority over this account.” Say what you are, accurately. Nothing more.
  3. “What do you need from me to record the death?” Let them talk. Write it down.
  4. “Does that include a certified death certificate, and do you return it?”

Then, before you hang up: “Can I have your first name, a direct extension, and a reference number for this call?” Have them repeat the number back. Put it in the phone log with the time.

An unlogged call did not happen. That was Chapter 1’s rule, and this is the week it stops being advice and starts being the difference between eleven minutes and three weeks.

The master list, in four tiers

Copy this onto the pad and fill in the names from your own parent’s mail and statements.
