This week, because money moves: Social Security, if the funeral home did not report it. The employer or former employer. Each pension or retirement plan. Each bank and credit union. Each brokerage. The life insurer. The health insurer, and the Advantage or Part D plan if there is one. The mortgage holder, if there is a mortgage. Home and auto insurers, if you have not already.

Next week: Credit card issuers. Any lender. The landlord, if there is one. Any professional association or union. The Department of Veterans Affairs, if your parent served, and Chapter 8 has the claim sheet for that.

Within the month: The state motor vehicle agency, by its own procedure, which you looked up in Chapter 4. Utilities, to change the account rather than to cancel it. Any government program paying into or out of the account.

Whenever you feel like it: everything else on your forty-one.

The point where you stop and call someone

Three things in this chapter mean you stop and get a lawyer on the phone before you make the next call, and I would rather say them plainly than have you find out in month three.

If a bank tells you they need Letters, or an order, or anything with the word “court” in it, that is a signal that the next step requires authority you may not have yet. If anyone asks you to sign a form that describes you as the executor, the administrator or the personal representative, and no court has appointed you, do not sign it. And if an insurer tells you the beneficiary on a policy is “the estate,” stop there, because where that money goes is a different question from who gets a check, and getting it wrong is expensive to undo.

A local estate lawyer can answer all three in a single paid hour. That is cheaper than any of them going wrong.

Next week the work goes quiet and turns to paper. Somewhere in that house there is a will, or there is not, and either way you are about to spend an afternoon opening drawers with somebody else in the room.

Get the reference number.

Chapter 6: Finding the Will and Everything Else

Week two started with Dale carrying a kitchen chair into Gene’s old office so two of us could reach the top shelf of the closet at the same time.

“Why two of us,” I said.

“Because if we find it, I want a witness who isn’t you,” he said. “Not that I don’t trust you. I don’t trust either of us alone with a long week behind it.”

He was right, and it is the first rule of this chapter before any list of places: do this with a second person in the room. Not because anyone expects a problem. Because grief plus a found document plus nobody else present is exactly the condition that turns an honest mistake into a fight six months later.

Where wills actually are

There is no national registry you call. A will lives in one of a short number of ordinary places, and you work through them in whatever order makes sense for your family.

The lawyer who drafted it, if anyone remembers a name or a firm. A home filing cabinet. A fireproof box, which in Gene and Helen’s house turned out to be a gray metal strongbox under the bed with a key taped to the inside of Helen’s jewelry box lid — not clever, just theirs. The person named as executor may already have a copy, or may know where the original sits. Some states let a person deposit a will with the county court for safekeeping while they’re alive, so a call to the county probate clerk asking whether one was filed costs you five minutes. And a bank safe deposit box.

The safe deposit box is the one that trips people up, because getting into it before an estate is formally opened depends on state law, and then on the bank’s own policy stacked on top of that. Some banks will let a named co-renter in with nothing more than a key and identification. Others won’t open a deceased person’s box to anyone, co-renter included, until a court has appointed someone. There is no single answer, and guessing wastes a trip. Call the bank, ask exactly what it requires to open the box, and get a name and a reference number for that call, in writing if they’ll give it to you. Write it in the phone log from Chapter 1.

We did not have a safe deposit box to deal with. Marlene did, for her husband’s, and she told me later that the bank asked her for something the county probate clerk hadn’t mentioned, and she lost a week finding that out the slow way. Ask both offices, not just one.

A deed or a tax return sitting in a desk drawer is simply there, waiting to be found by whoever opens the drawer. A safe deposit box has a lock, a key, and an institution with its own rules standing between you and the contents, and that institution did not know your family before this week and has no reason to make an exception for it. Treat the phone call to the bank as its own small errand, separate from the search through the house, and don’t let it become the thing that holds up everything else.

What else you’re looking for while you look

The will is the headline, but this is the week you also gather everything else that will matter for the next eleven, so look for it in the same pass instead of starting over later.

Deeds and titles to any real estate or vehicles. Tax returns — start with the most recent one you can find, and ask whoever prepares it later which years actually matter for this estate, because that answer depends on facts you don’t have yet. Insurance policies of every kind: life, health, long-term care, the small ones tucked in with homeowner’s paperwork. Statements for every bank, brokerage, retirement and pension account you can find, even old ones. Military discharge papers, if your parent served — they may help with the VA burial claim in Chapter 8, but start the claim even if you do not have them. Marriage and divorce decrees. An address book, a Rolodex, a sticky note taped inside a drawer — anything with names and account numbers on it that a stranger would throw away.

Gene kept everything in one gray metal box and nothing anywhere else, which made this easy. Helen, three years later, kept things in four different places, two of which Ruth found by accident — a manila envelope behind the encyclopedias, and a shoebox in the hall closet that also held, as it turned out, the pay stub from Chapter 5’s eleven-minute pension call. Your parents are probably somewhere between those two. Look slowly, with the second person, and don’t throw anything away this week that you can’t explain.

Touch it carefully

Once you find the will, do three things and avoid three others.

Do: read it once, calmly, before you decide anything about it. Do: note who is named executor, who are the beneficiaries, and who is named as an alternate if the first choice can’t serve. Do: make a photocopy for your own working file and put the original somewhere it cannot be lost, spilled on, or carried off in someone’s bag “just to look at it at home.”

Do not sign it, initial it, staple anything to it, or write on it. Not even a date in the margin, not even in pencil. Do not let anyone take the original out of the house, including the person named executor, until you’ve asked a lawyer whether that’s safe in your state. And do not assume the will is final just because it’s the only one you found. Look for a later date on a second document, a codicil, or language that says it revokes anything earlier.

Some states require the original will to be delivered to the probate court before anyone opens an estate, and the deadline can be short. Ask the probate clerk or an estate lawyer today what your state’s rule requires; the filing process itself is in The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide. This chapter’s job ends at finding it, reading it once, and keeping it safe.

What the will does not decide

A will may not control every asset; preserve any beneficiary or ownership record you find, and see Estate Planning for Beginners before anyone relies on it.

Reading it without panicking

The first time through, resist the urge to read every clause as a verdict on who was loved more. Wills are drafted in a lawyer’s language, written years before anyone involved was thinking about this week, and they often say less than they seem to. A phrase that sounds cold on a Tuesday afternoon in week two was usually just standard drafting language in 2004.

What you actually need from this first reading is three names: the person given the job of carrying this out, the people set to inherit, and whoever stands behind the first choice if that person can’t or won’t serve. Write those three things on the same page as your document inventory. Everything else in the will — specific bequests, trust language, contingent clauses — can wait for the lawyer who will eventually help whoever is executor open the estate. That’s a different conversation, and it belongs to a different week.

If something in the will surprises you, say so out loud to the person who was with you when you found it, and then set it aside rather than deciding what it means on your own at eleven at night. A surprising sentence read tired is rarely read accurately.

If there’s no will at all

If you search everywhere in this chapter and there genuinely isn’t one, your parent died “intestate,” and every state has a default order for who inherits in that situation. It is not chaos, and you are not stuck — it means the next step is reading your own state’s intestacy rules rather than a document your parent wrote. The probate clerk can point you to the current statute and local procedure, usually in one phone call. An estate lawyer can tell you how that statute applies to your family before anyone acts on it. It typically starts with a surviving spouse and children. The exact shares depend on how many of each there are, and whether any of the children came from a different relationship. Beyond that first ring, the rules diverge enough between states that naming one state’s answer here would do more harm than good to a reader somewhere else.

Nothing else about your week two changes: you still gather the documents, still keep the originals safe, and still start the box and the notebook. The absence of a will does not mean the absence of a plan. It means the plan was written by your state legislature instead of your parent, and someone can read it to you.

What “not found” actually means

A tick beside “desk” should mean somebody looked through the desk, not that somebody remembers your father saying he kept papers there. On the inventory’s reverse side, record the places actually checked and who checked them. Leave a separate entry for places you could not access. A locked box is an unfinished search, not an empty one.

Keep a loose document with the envelope or covering letter it came in. The return address may identify the office that can explain what you found. Don’t dismantle bundles to make a prettier pile before noting what was together.

Suppose the desk holds a photocopy marked “page 1 of 4,” but the other pages are missing. Record exactly that, along with its date and the location where you found it. Look for the rest among the nearby papers and contact the office named on the copy. Do not fill the gap with a relative’s recollection or label the copy “the will” as though the search were complete. An incomplete document needs assessment by the estate lawyer, not reconstruction at the kitchen table.

If someone says another folder went home with an aunt, record that lead and arrange a follow-up with her. You need to check that folder, not search the desk again.

The system that carries the next eleven weeks

Whatever you find, start the system here, this week, because you will be adding to it until day ninety.

One box for the original papers. One notebook or spreadsheet listing every document you found, with a column for found or not found and the date. A sibling calling from out of town can then ask “did we find the title to the Buick” and get an answer in one sentence, instead of sending someone through the house again.

Write down where each original now lives — the box, the drawer, whoever’s glove compartment it rode home in — and don’t throw anything away yet. What you can safely discard, and when, is a Chapter 12 question, not a week-two one.

The tool: the eight places to look, and a document inventory

Go through these in whatever order fits your family, with a second person present, and don’t skip ahead to “we probably don’t have one of those.”

  1. The lawyer who may have drafted it — a name on an old envelope, a bill, or a number saved in a phone counts as a lead.
  2. Home filing cabinet or desk.
  3. A fireproof box or strongbox, wherever it’s kept.
  4. The person named as executor, who may hold a copy or know where the original is.
  5. The county probate clerk, by phone, asking whether a will was deposited for safekeeping.
  6. A bank safe deposit box — call first and ask what the bank requires to open it.
  7. A digital folder or cloud account, if your parent was that kind of organized.
  8. Anywhere else papers lived: a nightstand, a closet shelf, a car’s glove box, a relative who was asked to “hold onto this.”

Then the document inventory, one line per item: deed, vehicle titles, tax returns (which years), life insurance policies, health and long-term care policies, bank and brokerage statements, pension and retirement paperwork, military discharge papers, marriage and divorce decrees, address book. Two columns next to each: found or not found, and the date you checked.

Helen’s house, in 2019, had a folder already made — tabbed, dated, sitting in the second kitchen drawer where she always said it was. It did not make the grief smaller. It made the week shorter, which is a different thing, and the only thing a folder can do.

Next week the envelopes start arriving in earnest, and not all of them are yours to pay.

Chapter 7: Which Bills to Pay, Which to Stop, and What to Freeze

By the third week after Gene died in March 2016, the mail stopped being a trickle. If you’re in weeks two to four now, this is the work on the kitchen table.

I had two envelopes from the same hospital on the kitchen table, six days apart, and they did not agree with each other. The first said Gene owed a little over four hundred dollars. The second, same account number, same dates of service, said eleven hundred and change. Neither one explained the other. Both had a due date printed in a box in the corner, and both were addressed to a man who had been dead for three weeks.

I sat there with my checkbook out. The invoice felt like something I’d left unfinished. Settling it felt like taking care of him one last time.

Dale came through, looked at the two amounts, and said, “Then it’s their arithmetic, not yours. Make them do it.”

I put the checkbook away.

Their estate, not your checking account

Their debts are generally paid from their estate, not your checking account.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s page “Does a person’s debt go away when they die?”, updated in September 2026, explains that debts are generally paid using the money or property the person left. If those assets cannot cover a debt and nobody else was legally responsible, the CFPB says it may remain unpaid. Survivors, including spouses, generally do not owe it unless they shared legal responsibility or another exception applies.

An unpaid debt can be a lawful outcome. You do not have to repair a shortfall merely because you’re the child answering the mail. Nor does this mean the estate can ignore a valid obligation. Those are different questions.

A balance on a statement establishes neither your personal responsibility nor permission to use your parent’s account. Before payment, someone must establish both the obligation and the authority to pay it.

The exceptions, one at a time

I promised early on that I would walk through the exceptions rather than wave at them. “There are exceptions” is how a frightened person ends up writing a check. The CFPB lists five situations where you may be responsible for someone else’s debt. Here they are, one at a time.

You co-signed a loan that still has debt outstanding. Your own agreement to repay matters; being the child who helped fill out the application is not the same thing.

You are a joint account holder on a credit card. The CFPB distinguishes this from being an authorized user. A card bearing your name does not, by itself, tell you which you are.

You are a surviving spouse and your state law requires spouses to pay that particular type of debt. Do not apply the adult child’s answer to the surviving parent’s bill without checking this exception.

You are the executor or administrator and your state law requires executors or administrators to pay an outstanding bill out of property that was jointly owned by the surviving and deceased spouses.

You are a surviving spouse in a community property state whose law requires jointly held property to be used for the deceased spouse’s debts. The CFPB names Alaska if a special agreement was signed, Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin. Living in a named state is a reason to check, not proof that every bill is yours.

California supplies a verified example, not a national rule. Its Probate Code section 13550, checked on the official California Legislative Information site in 2026, addresses surviving-spouse liability with property limits and exceptions. For your state, ask the probate clerk for the official statutes and a local estate lawyer how they apply to your family. A clerk can locate the rule; a lawyer can interpret it for you.

The Federal Trade Commission’s “Debts and Deceased Relatives”, dated February 2023 and checked again in 2026, adds a warning for the person handling the estate. Someone legally responsible for resolving it may become personally responsible by failing to follow certain state probate laws. The CFPB’s jointly owned-property exception is not permission to reach into your own account, and the FTC’s warning is not a reason to pay every envelope.

If no exception applies, the CFPB says the debt belongs only to the estate. Establish that answer rather than borrowing it from the loudest relative.

Authorized user is not co-signer

Suppose your parent added you to a card to buy groceries. Your name is embossed on the plastic, and now someone says that makes the balance yours.

The CFPB’s authorized-user answer, last modified in September 2024 and checked again in 2026, says that being an authorized user generally does not obligate you to pay. A joint borrower and a permitted user have different responsibilities.

If a collector claims you co-signed and you believe you did not, the CFPB says you may request evidence, such as the signed contract. That same page says issuers generally report authorized-user status to credit bureaus, so the relevant part of your own report may help establish your role. It describes a free report once each year from each nationwide bureau through annualcreditreport.com or 1-877-322-8228.

Ask for the contract. In writing.

That means your report, not an attempt to obtain or freeze your parent’s file. Chapter 10 owns deceased-consumer identity protection and collector conduct. Here you are answering a narrower question: did you agree to repay this debt?

The bill that came twice

Back to the two hospital envelopes.

I called billing with the Chapter 1 phone log open and asked why the amounts differed and which statement was current. The woman found an insurance adjustment, then a reversal, and a third statement already generated. I asked for the explanation and the corrected statement in writing.

The third statement, when it came, was for ninety-one dollars.

That was the amount the hospital was then asking for, not proof that I owed it personally or that it could be paid ahead of other claims. A corrected amount still needed the same authority check. My checkbook remained shut.

For a medical statement, ask what services it covers, whether insurance has finished processing, and whether it replaces an earlier statement. Have billing identify what it needs from an authorized person if it cannot discuss the account with you. Keep the old statement beside the new one; crossing out the old balance does not explain what happened.

What to stop, and what to leave alone

Use the empty-house safeguards from Chapter 4 without doing that walkthrough again. This question sorts the recurring charges: does the payment still protect something or provide a service someone needs?

If not, mark it for cancellation by the person the provider authorizes. If it protects property, a claim, records or a survivor’s coverage, get instructions before stopping it. An unfamiliar charge is not automatically useless.

A magazine nobody reads, a delivery box, or an unused membership is a candidate. A family streaming account may still serve the surviving parent. A storage subscription may hold the only copies of photographs. Do not cancel by the shape of the company name alone.

Tell the provider about the death using the Chapter 5 notification approach. Ask who may cancel, what documents it needs, when charges stop, and whether a remaining balance or contractual commitment exists. Get confirmation.

The CFPB’s automatic-payments guidance, updated in August 2026, distinguishes cancelling a debit from cancelling the underlying contract or amount owed. That guidance describes your own account; it does not give an adult child authority over a deceased parent’s account. Cancelling future service also does not establish that earlier charges are invalid.

Do not use your parent’s login or sign as their representative to make the charges disappear. Ask the bank or provider for the procedure your actual role permits. Let the person with authority coordinate autopay changes; shutting down an account wholesale can interrupt payments you meant to preserve.

For heat, insurance, a mortgage, rent or storage holding belongings, identify the next due date and any threatened interruption. Ask the appointed representative or estate lawyer who can authorize payment, which necessary payments should continue, and what account can lawfully fund them. The estate account, creditor-claim procedure and payment priorities belong to The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

Do not advance personal money because an envelope sounds urgent. If nobody is appointed and a lapse would endanger property, tell the lawyer that today. Ask the provider about an extension or temporary arrangement while authority is clarified; do not assume one exists. Keep necessary service in place through an authorized arrangement, not by promising personally to cover an unknown balance.

Open it, date it, put it down

Holding a bill means withholding payment while someone checks it. It does not mean ignoring its dates.

Read the mail you are entitled to handle as it arrives. Date your working copy or envelope, leaving original legal documents unmarked. Put any due date, hearing date or threatened service interruption on the list beside the bill. Route court papers and notices with response dates promptly to the representative and lawyer; a hold pile does not stop a clock.

Medical and credit card statements can wait for verification and the authorized payment decision, but not unseen in a drawer. Ask what is unresolved and who will check it. Record a follow-up date. If a bill arrives after you asked a question, attach it to the same record rather than starting a second, disconnected pile.

There is no national waiting period in this chapter. “Don’t pay yet” means verify and route, not leave every debt untouched until day ninety. When you hand a bill over, note who received it and when. If nobody accepts responsibility for checking it, you still have an open item.

Keep the receipts you think are too small to matter

If you’ve already spent your own money, start a separate expense record.

The county-office parking, locksmith and certified copies all get entries. So does a funeral deposit you personally paid. Keep personal purchases separate; a meal for relatives is not automatically an estate expense because you ate it while doing paperwork.

For each expense, record what it bought, when, who paid, and who authorized it, if anyone. Keep the receipt and evidence of payment together. Send the record promptly to the representative and ask what documentation and timing apply to a reimbursement request. Do not wait for the estate to finish before asking.

Reimbursement depends on the applicable law, the expense and what the estate can pay. I cannot promise it. Do not deduct your expenses from money you are holding or pay yourself back without confirmed authority. Recording a cost preserves the question; it does not decide it.

The tool: the four-pile sort

Clear the table. Take every envelope that has arrived since the death, plus everything you have already opened and shoved somewhere, and put each one into one of four piles.

Ask: who owes this, and what establishes that obligation? If you cannot answer, the bill is not ready for payment. Check response dates before sorting.

  1. Route for authorized payment. The obligation has been checked. Give it to the authorized person for the payment decision, noting due dates and any unresolved issue. This is a handoff, not permission to pay it yourself or evidence that it takes priority.
  2. Hold, unpaid. The amount, insurance processing or legal responsibility remains unclear. Add the person checking it and a follow-up date. Send time-sensitive notices onward even while the balance is unresolved.
  3. Challenge in writing. Request an explanation of a disputed amount or obligation. If a collector claims you co-signed, request the evidence described above. Keep your copy and follow the notice’s applicable response instructions with legal help where needed.
  4. Not an estate obligation. Use this only when you have established that fact: an optional sales offer is one example. A renewal may instead reflect an existing contract. If the bill is yours personally, route it to your own records; this pile does not make it disappear.

Beside each item, note its pile, who has it and the next action date. Tomorrow’s envelope can then join an existing question instead of becoming another mystery.

Where this stops being a paperwork problem

Call a local estate lawyer before committing money if a collector claims you’re personally liable, a jointly owned house has a mortgage, or the known assets cannot cover the bills. Bring the account agreement or loan papers if you have them. These are questions about liability, ownership and payment order, not how carefully you balance a checkbook.

The CFPB’s September 2026 guidance says a collector may discuss estate debts with a surviving spouse or personal representative, but cannot falsely suggest personal liability when no exception applies. Being asked about a bill does not establish that you owe it. Have the lawyer identify the legal basis before you agree to pay, sign a repayment plan or supply your own card number.

If the estate appears short of money, do not select creditors by whose letter sounds angriest. Get advice before making payments. The FTC’s probate-law warning is why doing the work carefully includes knowing when to stop.

Ask for a defined consultation and its fee in writing. For a disputed collection demand, ask whether consumer-law or debt-collection-defense help is also needed. The CFPB points readers to local lawyer referrals and legal aid for people who meet eligibility criteria; paying a private lawyer is not the only route to ask about.

Put the two statements together in the folder. Write who will check them and when. Leave the checkbook where it is.

Chapter 8: Government Benefits to Check

It’s week three or four, and you’re standing at the refrigerator with an appointment card in one hand and a pen that won’t write in the other.

The funeral is behind you. Someone has taken the flowers away. The calendar still has your parent’s haircut on it, but nothing about applying for a benefit. You have to put that there yourself.

Missing a claim need not mean someone was careless. A family can do every task it was given and still miss the task nobody mentioned.

Start with Chapter 5’s notification contacts. This time you’re asking whether a living person can claim a benefit, and what must happen next.

The small payment with its own clock

The Social Security Administration’s “Lump-sum death payment” page, checked in October 2026, gives the amount as $255, paid once. It is not an allowance payable to whichever adult child arranged the funeral.

SSA says a spouse might qualify. A spouse who wasn’t living in the same home may still qualify if eligible for benefits on the deceased person’s record. Separate addresses, including a care facility, are a reason to ask, not a reason to cross the claim off.

If there is no eligible spouse, certain children may qualify. SSA’s 2026 guidance describes children age 17 or younger; children ages 18 to 19 attending school full time at the K-12 level; and children of any age whose disability developed at age 21 or younger. Being an adult child without that qualifying disability does not establish eligibility because you bought the casket or handled the paperwork.

According to that same SSA page in 2026, you must apply within two years of the death. The clock starts with the death, not the burial, not the date the certificate arrived, and not the day you found this chapter. Put the death date and the resulting deadline on your claim sheet.

For this payment, SSA’s page currently offers an online application through the applicant’s account. It also tells you to call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) and say you want to apply for the lump-sum death payment. Start at ssa.gov and follow its link; don’t use your parent’s login.

If you’re helping the surviving parent, ask SSA how you may assist and what the claimant needs to do personally.

A monthly benefit is a separate question

Survivor benefits can provide monthly income based on the deceased person’s Social Security work record. SSA’s 2026 survivor guidance identifies possible claimants as spouses, former spouses, children and dependent parents. This is a benefit for an eligible survivor, not an estate asset available to divide among siblings.

Check both payments. Give each its own entry so that a yes about one cannot become a remembered yes about both.

Under SSA’s eligibility page checked in 2026, a surviving spouse may qualify at age 60 or older, or at ages 50 to 59 with a qualifying disability. The general marriage-duration requirement is at least nine months before the death. SSA also describes restrictions involving remarriage before age 60, or before age 50 for someone with a disability.

Those are screening rules, not the whole decision. SSA names exceptions involving age and marriage duration, including some cases where the survivor cares for the deceased person’s child. Tell SSA about that care and the child’s circumstances rather than ruling the survivor out by age alone.

SSA’s 2026 page says a former spouse whose marriage lasted at least ten years may qualify. Certain valid non-marital legal relationships may qualify too. Bring the marriage and divorce history into the conversation. It is not your job to decide whether an earlier marriage counts from a sentence somebody remembers.

For children, SSA’s 2026 eligibility guidance gives the same basic age, school and disability categories described above, generally with an unmarried requirement. It also recognizes certain circumstances involving married children, adopted children, stepchildren, grandchildren and stepgrandchildren. An adult child’s disability must have begun before their twenty-second birthday; needing help only later in adulthood does not establish that condition.

There is another person worth remembering: your parent’s surviving parent. SSA’s 2026 page identifies dependent parents age 62 or older who were financially supported by the child who died as possible claimants. If your father was helping pay his mother’s rent, tell SSA and ask what support evidence is required.

Get an estimate before choosing a starting month

The size of a survivor payment depends on the claimant’s circumstances. Your parent’s last deposit is not a reliable calculation by itself.

SSA’s “What you could get from Survivor benefits” page, checked in 2026, says spouse and ex-spouse payments can start at 71.5% of the deceased spouse’s benefit. Its illustrations rise above 75% at age 61, above 80% at age 63, and above 90% at age 65. The page gives up to 100% at survivor full retirement age, which is between ages 66 and 67 depending on birth date.

Ask SSA for an estimate using the survivor’s actual record, birth date, work and marital history. These percentages aren’t your household’s quote.

For children, SSA’s 2026 amount page says the payment is generally 75% of the parent’s benefit, subject to a family maximum that may reduce payments. Former spouses do not count toward that maximum. If several people may qualify, mention all of them and ask for the calculation rather than multiplying a percentage yourself.

SSA also says in 2026 that survivor and other Social Security benefits are not added together as two full payments. A person eligible for both chooses the payment that is best for them, and switching later may be possible. SSA gives the example of taking survivor benefits and later switching to a higher retirement benefit at age 70; confirm the sequence and available dates before filing.

The claiming-age comparisons and breakeven calculations belong to Social Security, Claimed On Purpose in the Plain Talk Retirement Series; here, get SSA’s individualized estimates and establish the available claim before choosing its start date.

Call promptly to ask which filing and starting dates apply. Do not borrow the lump-sum payment’s two-year deadline for the monthly benefit. Tell SSA if the survivor is still working; its amount page warns that earnings limits may temporarily reduce payments depending on age.

Make the application real

SSA’s adult survivor application guidance, checked in 2026, directs you to call its national number and say “Survivor.” It may help you file during that call or arrange an appointment. The online lump-sum application is not an instruction to file every kind of survivor claim online.

That guidance also says people already receiving Social Security Family benefits generally have their benefit type and amount updated automatically. If that describes the surviving parent, ask SSA to confirm what is changing and whether anything remains to be filed. Already receiving one’s own retirement payment is not the same description.

Use SSA’s Form SSA-10 information page for a surviving spouse or former spouse, and its Form SSA-8 information page for the lump-sum claim. Both were checked in 2026. They name documents SSA may request, including proof of death and birth; the spouse’s page also names the marriage certificate and, where relevant, a final divorce decree. Ask for the document list for the actual claimant rather than treating those pages as one universal packet.

SSA accepts photocopies of some records, such as wage statements, but requires originals of many others and says it returns them. Use the certificate tracking from Chapter 3 without redoing the count here. Confirm the submission route and the return arrangement before sending valuable originals.

Both SSA information pages tell applicants not to delay a claim because documents are missing; the agency will help obtain them. Call with the papers you have. Say which are missing. Record whether you have filed, merely booked an appointment, or still owe an action. A date written beside “called” is not proof of submission.

Ask about VA monthly survivor income

VA’s “Survivors Pension and D.I.C.” guidance, checked in October 2026, identifies surviving spouses, children and parents as possible claimants for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC). Its Survivors Pension page describes monthly payments for qualifying surviving spouses and unmarried dependent children of wartime Veterans, subject to income and net worth limits. Have VA check the survivor’s circumstances rather than treating a discharge paper as approval.

If your parent served, ask VA or a VA-accredited VSO representative whether the survivor should also apply for DIC or Survivors Pension, and whether to submit an intent to file now; these are separate from the burial allowance and may have different eligibility and payment start dates.

VA’s “Your intent to file a VA claim” page, checked in October 2026, says an intent to file may protect a potential earlier start date if the claim is approved. Give DIC and Survivors Pension separate claim-sheet entries from burial benefits. Record any intent-to-file confirmation and ask VA for the deadline to complete that claim; an intent to file is not the completed application.

VA money begins with eligibility, not a receipt

A military discharge paper makes this worth checking. It does not, by itself, make every funeral bill eligible for reimbursement.

The Department of Veterans Affairs’ “Veterans burial allowance and transportation benefits” page, updated October 1, 2026, describes separate routes. For a family-filed burial or transportation claim, ask VA who may claim the costs paid and which reimbursements affect eligibility. VA separately describes an automatic set payment for an eligible surviving spouse listed on the Veteran’s profile; confirm what it covers before assuming no claim is needed for other expenses.

Its claimant categories include surviving spouses or qualifying legal-union partners, children, parents, estate representatives, other family members or friends, and representatives of funeral homes or cemeteries.

The Veteran’s circumstances matter too. VA says the Veteran must not have received a dishonorable discharge and must meet a qualifying condition. Its page includes service-connected death, death during VA or VA-contracted care, certain VA-authorized travel, receipt of VA pension or compensation, and certain pending claims that would have established entitlement. It also describes cases where military retirement pay was received instead of VA benefits. Have VA check the actual history.

The same 2026 page excludes burial allowances for someone who died on active duty, while serving in Congress, or while serving a federal prison sentence. Ask about other applicable benefits separately.

Using Chapter 7’s expense record, identify who paid and any organizational reimbursement. Ask VA which claimant and costs fit its rules before relatives submit overlapping claims.

Match the VA amount to the death date

VA’s October 1, 2026 rate page lists a non-service-connected burial allowance of $1,032 and a plot allowance of $1,032 for eligible deaths on or after October 1, 2026. For deaths from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026, the listed amounts are $1,002 each. For deaths from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025, they are $978 each.

Ask VA to identify the applicable category and amount; neither allowance is promised to every claimant. Filing this October for an earlier death does not acquire the newest rate.

Check the date.

For service-connected deaths, VA’s 2026 page lists $2,000 for deaths on or after September 11, 2001, and $1,500 for earlier deaths. Service connected means the death was due to an illness or injury caused or made worse by active-duty service. Do not substitute “served in the military” for that finding.

The same VA page, as checked in 2026, lists a headstone or marker allowance of $441 for deaths on or after October 1, 2025. Ask whether that allowance applies in your case. VA also has a separate government-headstone and marker program with its own eligibility and application; buying a stone does not establish a right to a refund. Check before committing that money.

The VA clock has exceptions

VA’s October 2026 guidance gives no filing time limit for burial or transportation allowances when the death was service connected. For a non-service-connected death, the burial claim generally must be filed within two years after burial. Notice the starting event: burial, not death.

VA’s 2026 page makes exceptions. There is no filing time limit for a non-service-connected death while under VA care at a VA health facility or a VA-contracted facility. There is also no time limit for the plot or interment allowance, or transportation allowance. If VA changed a dishonorable discharge status after death to another status, its page gives a two-year filing period from that change.

Have VA confirm any exception and keep evidence of the relevant burial date, care setting or discharge-status change. Write ‘no filing limit’ on the claim sheet only after VA confirms the exception applies to this claim.

According to VA’s 2026 guidance, death notification triggers the automatic set payment for a qualifying spouse recorded in the Veteran’s profile. That spouse need not apply for this payment. Confirm that the spouse is listed, what payment is being handled, and whether additional claimed costs need an application. Do not assume the child who paid the bill will automatically receive money, or that an automatic payment answers every claim.

Put the VA papers together

You can apply online through va.gov or mail VA Form 21P-530EZ, Application for Burial Benefits. VA’s October 2026 instructions give the mailing destination as Department of Veterans Affairs, Pension Intake Center, PO Box 5365, Janesville, WI 53547-5365. Confirm that address on the current form before mailing.

The VA page says you may need the death certificate including cause of death and an itemized transportation receipt if you paid to move the remains. It recommends a copy of the DD214 or other separation documents covering all service periods; it does not say a missing DD214 means you cannot begin. Follow its military-records request link and ask how to proceed while the record is being obtained.

For a service-connected claim, VA recommends supporting medical records and explains how to authorize their release if you lack access. Use those instructions or ask for help; don’t claim authority to obtain records that you do not have.

Questions go to 1-800-827-1000 (TTY 711), listed by VA in 2026. If eligibility, discharge history or a denial is disputed, contact a VA-accredited representative before trying to interpret it alone. VA’s September 2026 representative guidance says accredited Veterans Service Organization representatives help with benefit claims free of charge. Accredited attorneys and claims agents may charge fees; confirm any arrangement before appointing someone.

Keep national-cemetery eligibility separate from cash allowances. VA’s national-cemetery guidance, checked in 2026, includes qualifying Veterans, spouses, minor children and some unmarried adult dependent children; surviving spouses may qualify even after remarriage. Ask about eligibility and availability if burial arrangements remain open. VA also lists bereavement counseling for certain eligible families; Chapter 11 covers asking for that help.

The employer still owes you an answer

Return to the pension contact already identified in Chapter 5. This is the follow-up, not another search through the house. Known employer and pension plans belong on this sheet too; the lost-pension search belongs to Chapter 9.

Send a short written request asking four things: who may qualify for a survivor payment; what the plan’s existing survivor election provides; which application and evidence it requires; and what filing date or other deadline applies. Ask the administrator to identify the governing plan document and confirm the answer in writing.

Plan terms and existing elections matter; do not assume a survivor can choose a different payout now. If the response addresses only the death notification, repeat the unanswered claim questions. If an entitlement or rejection is disputed, ask a lawyer who handles employee benefits to review it before a response deadline expires.

The tool: the benefits claim sheet

Use a separate page for each possible benefit and claimant. An empty deadline line remains an open question, not permission to wait.

  1. Benefit and claimant. Name the payment, the agency or known plan, and the person who might qualify. Mark eligibility as unconfirmed until you have an answer.
  2. Application route. Record the form or agency-directed process. Note who must sign and how you may help in your actual role.
  3. Clock. Copy the agency’s applicable rule, its starting event and that event’s date. Add the calculated deadline, source page and date checked, or the confirmed no-time-limit exception.
  4. Evidence. List required documents, which are missing, and how each will be obtained. Track originals through the Chapter 3 record.
  5. Submission. Record when and how you filed. Keep the submitted copy, confirmation or mailing evidence. Record an appointment separately.
  6. Next action. Name who will follow up and when. Record any evidence request, decision, response deadline or unresolved question.

For example, a VA burial claim uses the burial date. A plot claim gets its own deadline treatment. The SSA lump-sum claim uses the death date. Keep the source beside each entry so the clocks cannot swap places.

Take the appointment card off the refrigerator. Put it in the claimant’s folder, and write what that appointment is for.

Chapter 9: The Policy Nobody Knew About

Seven weeks after my mother died, a letter came to the farmhouse from a company she had stopped working for in 1991.

It was addressed to Helen, the way those letters always are. No logo I recognized, a return address in Columbus, and I came close to putting it on the advertising pile. Inside was one page about a group life certificate, a number across the top, and a phone number under that.

She had never mentioned it. Not in 2019, sitting at the kitchen table going through the folder she had made for us. Not in the thirty years before. I don’t believe she remembered it existed.

The amount was modest. But it was real, and it had been sitting somewhere since the first Bush administration.

The letter was found because someone was still opening the mail in week seven.

You are probably somewhere in weeks two to four. Start these searches now, because the answers take far longer to come back than the questions take to ask.

What this chapter is, and what it isn’t

Chapter 6 was the paper search: the eight places to look, the document inventory, the boxes in the closet. Chapter 4 set up the mail so it keeps arriving somewhere a person will read it. This chapter is the other half, the part you cannot do by opening a drawer.

This chapter gives you six no-cost routes: official government searches, regulator-linked tools, and an association-run multi-state search that sends matches back to state programs. Nobody has to be paid to run them. I will name each one, say what it covers and what it does not, and then hand you a sheet to record the date and result of each search.

I am also going to tell you how to claim a policy you already know about, because that one has traps in it too.

The policy you do know about

Start with whatever turned up in the document inventory: a policy booklet, a premium notice, a benefits summary from an employer, a certificate like Helen’s.

Find two things on it. The policy or certificate number, and the name of the insurance company.

Then find out whether that company still exists under that name. Insurers merge and get bought, and the name printed on a 1988 policy may belong to nobody now. Your state insurance department can help you work out who holds the book of business today. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners says every US state, the District of Columbia and the five US territories has a department of insurance whose job includes helping consumers; the NAIC indexes all of them on its consumer pages at naic.org.

When you reach the insurer, do not open with a claim. Open with a question: what does your company need, and from whom?

Ask who it treats as the claimant on this policy. Ask what form that person has to sign, and whether a different person can start the process. Ask what proof of death it accepts, whether that includes a certified copy, and whether it returns the copy afterward. That last pair is the same question from Chapter 3’s certificate count, and the answer goes on the same sheet.

Life insurance money goes to whoever the beneficiary designation names. Chapter 6 covered why that designation sits outside the will. What matters this week is that you do not promise anyone a share of money that is not yours to divide, including yourself.

Three situations mean you stop and get advice before anybody signs anything: the named beneficiary died before your parent did, the designation is blank or illegible, or two people both believe the policy is theirs. Ask the insurer in writing who it treats as the claimant and on what basis, then take that written answer to an estate lawyer. A signed release is hard to walk back.

If the insurer stops answering

Insurers are not all the same, and some of them get slow once the file leaves the first desk.

Give the company a fair chance first. The NAIC’s guidance on filing a complaint says to try to resolve the problem with the insurer before going over its head. Keep a record of every call and letter with dates and times, which is what the phone log has been doing since Chapter 1.

If that fails, your state department of insurance investigates complaints at no charge. The NAIC lists unfair claim delays, denials, failure to honor a policy and a lack of timely communication among the things a department can look at. Its filing advice is practical: gather the policy number and your documentation, complete the department’s complaint form, write a factual account that sticks to what happened and when, use the policy’s own language where you can, and say what outcome you want. The NAIC also says an insurer cannot discriminate against you later for having complained.

A complaint is a record of the issue for the state department. Keep the complaint number, every attachment and the insurer’s written response.

The free hunt for policies nobody mentioned

Now the harder case: you think there might be a policy, and you have no paper at all.

The NAIC runs the Life Insurance Policy Locator. Its own consumer page describes it as a free tool that helps beneficiaries search for unclaimed life insurance policies. Start at naic.org, follow the link from the consumer section, and read what it asks for before you begin.

It is free. Say that part twice to the relative who forwarded you an advertisement.

I cannot tell you how long it takes to hear back, or which companies it reaches, because the NAIC does not publish either of those as a promise. Run it, write the date you ran it on your sheet, and keep going with the rest of the list.

Money a state is already holding

Unclaimed property is where a forgotten savings account, an uncashed refund check or a utility deposit from 1996 ends up after the company holding it gives up on finding the owner. It does not disappear. It goes to a state program.

The National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators, a network of the National Association of State Treasurers, keeps an index of every state’s official program at unclaimed.org. NAUPA also runs MissingMoney.com, a free site that searches participating states at once and links you to the official state program when there is a match.

NAUPA states the position plainly: there is no fee to search for and claim unclaimed property through your state’s official program.

Search every state your parent ever lived or worked in. The state where they died is one of several. Search a maiden name. Search the name with a middle initial and without one, and search the obvious misspelling that a payroll clerk might have typed in 1978.

NAUPA’s page on searching beyond your state also points to federal sources families rarely think of. Unclaimed insured deposits from closed banks go through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Accounts from liquidated credit unions go through the National Credit Union Administration. Matured savings bonds sit with Treasury, and mortgage insurance refunds with the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

Whether a particular state will release property to you, and what it requires first, is set by that state’s program. Read its claim instructions before you fill anything in.

A pension that outlived the company

If your parent worked somewhere with a pension and that employer is gone, the money may not be.

The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation keeps a plan search at pbgc.gov covering trusteed plans and plans paying PBGC premiums. PBGC cautions that a plan’s payment of premiums does not by itself prove PBGC coverage or that a benefit is due. Treat a result as a lead, then ask the listed contact what plan applies and whether any benefit is payable. Each entry gives the sponsor’s name, its employer identification number, the plan number and a contact telephone number. Use the sponsor, plan number and contact number as leads. Ask the contact whether it administers the plan, who may ask about a deceased participant, and what authority it requires.

PBGC also keeps a separate database of unclaimed retirement benefits: money that went unpaid to people whose plans ended. PBGC’s page says the database is updated quarterly and names the date of the most recent update, which was August 5, 2026 when I looked. The search asks for a last name and the last four digits of a Social Security number, and PBGC prints a privacy notice explaining what it does with that. Read the notice, and ask PBGC how a survivor or a representative should proceed rather than guessing. PBGC publishes its own pages on eligibility, on what to do before contacting it, and on the documents needed to claim a benefit.

A known employer plan is different work. That one belongs on the claim sheet from Chapter 8, where you are chasing an administrator who already has your parent’s file.

If your parent served

The Department of Veterans Affairs keeps an unclaimed funds search of its own at insurance.va.gov, and it has nothing to do with the burial money in Chapter 8.

VA says these are insurance funds owed to certain current or former policyholders, or to their beneficiaries, where VA has been unable to locate the person to make payment. The page lists the older programs involved, with names like National Service Life Insurance and Veterans Special Life Insurance. VA states on that same page that the search does not include Servicemembers’ Group Life Insurance or Veterans’ Group Life Insurance policies from 1965 to the present, and tells holders of those policies not to use it.

It takes a last name. If your father or mother served, run it.

The people who want a percentage

Somewhere around month two, a letter may arrive from a company that has found money in your parent’s name and would like to recover it for you.

Run every free search in this chapter first.

NAUPA is direct about this. Third-party finders and locators do exist, they often charge a percentage of what is recovered, and in most cases they are operating legally. NAUPA also says that many states require finders to register or hold a licence, that some states cap the fee, and that all of the same information is available at no charge through the state’s own program or MissingMoney.com. Its advice before you sign anything is to contact your state’s unclaimed property office and check the finder.

That is my advice too, extended one step. Before you agree to anything with anyone who contacted you first, verify the asset directly with the agency, insurer or plan that supposedly holds it. Then get the fee, the scope and the authorization terms in writing, and read what you are authorizing them to sign on your behalf.

Pressure does not prove fraud, but it is a reason to pause. Verify the asset directly with the holder and read the proposed fee, scope and authorization before signing.

The day something actually turns up

You find a policy. A state says it is holding eleven hundred dollars. The letter from 1991 lands on your kitchen table.

Do nothing with it yet.

Write it down: what it is, who says it exists, the reference number, the date you learned about it, and what the holder says it requires. Then work out whose money it is before a dollar moves. A payment to a named beneficiary and an asset belonging to the estate are two different things with two different sets of rules, and the person who has to sort that out is whoever has authority. What the estate then does with an asset is The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide, not this book.

Tell the appointed representative about anything you find, promptly, even if you are sure it is a beneficiary payment. A found asset can change the answer to Chapter 7’s question about whether the estate can cover what it owes.

And do not deposit a check made out to your dead parent into your own account. Ask the bank what the person with authority has to do instead.

The tool: the found-money sweep

One page. Six searches. Beside each one, write what it needs before you start, the date you ran it, and what came back.

  1. The policy you have. Insurer’s current name and the policy or certificate number. Call and ask what it needs and from whom. Record the claimant, the form, the proof of death and whether documents come back.
  2. The NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator. Free, from naic.org’s consumer section. Read its requirements first. Write the submission date.
  3. Your state’s official unclaimed property program. Found through unclaimed.org. Free. Run it for your own state first because that is the one you can telephone.
  4. MissingMoney.com. Free, run by NAUPA, several states at once. Search every state your parent lived or worked in, plus the maiden name and the likely misspelling.
  5. PBGC. The plan search at pbgc.gov for a plan whose sponsor you can name, and the unclaimed retirement benefits database for a benefit that went unpaid. Read PBGC’s privacy notice and ask how a survivor should proceed.
  6. VA unclaimed funds, at insurance.va.gov, if your parent served. Not the burial allowance, and not SGLI or VGLI.

Write a future review date on the sheet if new mail, employer records or a state-program instruction gives you a reason to search again.

Keep reading mail while forwarding is active and while claims, account questions, and the searches on this sheet remain open. Put a review date beside each open item.

Chapter 10: Protecting a Dead Person From Fraud

By month two, you may be sitting beside your parent’s phone, watching it ring and wondering whether answering it will create another job.

Marlene got a call three days after her husband’s funeral. The caller knew his full name and date of birth. He wanted her to fetch his Medicare card so he could “finish the file.”

She left the card in the drawer.

She brought a question across the road afterward: how did he have the birthday?

Knowing a birthday does not prove someone works for Medicare or a bank. A public death notice can supply details. So can other records. You need not discover where the caller found them before refusing to supply more.

You want to prevent identity misuse without losing the photographs or messages worth keeping. Closing everything at once can work against that.

The notice does not need the whole biography

If the obituary is still being written, leave out the street address, full birth date and mother’s maiden name. You can describe a life without supplying every detail someone might use to impersonate that person. A town, a year and the people who mattered can do the work.

Tell whoever submits the notice which details you want withheld. Check the version that will go online, not just the paragraph your cousin sent you. Avoid publishing photographs of certificates, identity cards or paperwork with account numbers visible.

During a funeral or memorial service, ask someone you trust to stay at the otherwise empty house. Keep the arrangement private. Chapter 4’s empty-house safeguards still apply.

If sensitive details are already online, ask the publisher what it can remove. Editing the page may not erase copies elsewhere. Don’t blame yourself for a notice written while you were barely sleeping. Start with what remains under your control.

Ask the bureaus about a deceased consumer

The Federal Trade Commission’s “What To Know About Identity Theft,” dated September 2024 and checked again in October 2026, explains credit freezes and fraud alerts for people protecting their own reports. It does not establish your authority to put either on your dead parent’s file.

Use the FTC’s IdentityTheft.gov credit-bureau contact page to reach Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. As checked in October 2026, it lists Equifax at 1-800-685-1111; Experian at 1-888-397-3742 (1-888-EXPERIAN); and TransUnion at 1-888-909-8872. These are contact points, not a deceased-consumer application procedure.

Contact each bureau. State that the consumer has died and describe your actual role. Ask for its current deceased-consumer instructions and required proof of authority in writing. Follow that bureau’s directions, using the secure submission route it identifies; do not send identity papers to an address supplied by an unsolicited caller.

Do not request a freeze or alert in your parent’s name unless the bureau confirms in writing that you may and explains what it requires. Do not describe yourself as executor if that is not your role. Being the child who found the statement does not settle the authority question.

Ask how the authorized person can later review the file, report an unfamiliar account and confirm that the bureau processed the death notice. Request a reference number and a follow-up date. Put the answer in Chapter 1’s phone log rather than keeping it in your head.

Do not borrow a living consumer’s checklist and change the name. Get the applicable instructions from each company.

An unfamiliar bill needs checking, not guessing

A new account notice, an unexplained withdrawal or a bill for something your parent never bought needs prompt attention. The FTC’s identity-theft guidance names unfamiliar bills and transactions as warning signs. They are reasons to investigate, not proof that every late envelope is fraudulent.

Keep the envelope and the notice. Record the account identifier, the transaction date and what seems wrong. Pass the evidence promptly to the person with authority over the affected account. Verify the business through contact details obtained independently, such as its official website or an earlier genuine statement. Ask its fraud team how to report a deceased customer’s suspected identity theft and what evidence it needs.

For identity theft that appears to have occurred, go to IdentityTheft.gov. The FTC’s guidance checked in 2026 says the site provides a free recovery plan and prepared letters and forms. Spanish reporting is available at RobodeIdentidad.gov; the FTC lists 1-877-438-4338 for telephone help, including other languages.

State the death and your role. If the site’s choices don’t fit, call for guidance rather than describing yourself as the victim. Reporting suspected theft does not give you account access or let you sign for the estate.

If money is moving without authorization, contact the institution’s fraud staff now. Ask what protective action it can take and what the authorized representative must do next. Don’t wait for the checklist below.

A collector’s call has boundaries

Chapter 7 dealt with whether a debt is yours. A genuine debt can still be collected improperly; an unpleasant call does not establish that the bill is fake.

In its debt-collection law guidance rechecked in 2026, the CFPB describes the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act as covering personal, family and household debts. It generally does not cover the original creditor collecting its own debt or business debts. The protections below concern collectors covered by that law; ask your state attorney general about additional state protections.

In its February 2023 guidance “Debts and Deceased Relatives,” rechecked in 2026, the FTC distinguishes debt discussions from requests to locate the estate representative. Permitted discussion roles include the surviving spouse, a deceased minor’s parent, legal guardian, lawyer, authorized estate representative and a mortgage servicer’s confirmed successor in interest. Being an adult child alone is not one of those roles.

A collector may contact relatives without that authority to obtain the representative’s contact information, but the FTC says it cannot discuss the debt’s details with them. The guidance describes limited circumstances allowing a further contact. It is not an invitation to repeatedly argue the balance with whichever child answers the phone.

If you are only helping locate the representative, say that. Do not negotiate or promise payment. If you are the representative, get the written information before addressing the demand, and use the four-pile sort from Chapter 7 for the resulting papers.

The CFPB’s deceased-debt guidance, updated September 2026, says collectors must provide validation information during the first communication or within five days. A validation notice identifies the collector and creditor, the account if applicable, the current amount and its itemization, and how to respond. Its validation page, rechecked in 2026, also requires the dispute period’s end date.

According to that CFPB validation page in 2026, the written-dispute period is 30 days. A timely written dispute requires the collector to pause collection of the disputed amount until it adequately responds. Give the notice promptly to the authorized representative to confirm the deadline and act. A telephone objection or filing the bill away does not have the same effect. This is not the estate’s probate claim deadline.

The CFPB’s harassment guidance, also checked in 2026, says the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibits harassment, oppression and abuse. It names repeated communications intended to harass, abusive language, false arrest threats and misrepresentations about the amount owed. Preserve messages and written demands; note what was said during calls without assuming you may record a conversation under your state’s law.

Complaints can go to consumerfinance.gov/complaint or your state attorney general’s consumer-protection office. State collection laws can differ; ask that office about yours. California’s attorney general, for example, publishes collection guidance at oag.ca.gov but says the office cannot provide individual legal assistance. If there are threats, disputed signing authority or court papers, call a consumer or estate lawyer promptly to establish the response deadline. A complaint does not answer a lawsuit.

The probate claim process belongs to The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide; this chapter does not set the estate’s payment order or court timetable.

The Medicare card stays out of the conversation

Medicare.gov’s fraud-and-abuse page, checked in October 2026, tells readers to protect their Medicare and Social Security numbers. It says Medicare will not call to sell something or visit your home. It also describes limited situations in which Medicare or someone representing it may return a call and request information. “Medicare never calls” is therefore the wrong test.

End an unverified call and contact the agency yourself through its published number.

Report suspected Medicare fraud at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), or use the HHS Office of Inspector General’s reporting page at oig.hhs.gov/fraud/report-fraud/. Those routes are listed on Medicare.gov in 2026. Say that the beneficiary has died and ask how you should supply the information.

Check statements you may lawfully review against the service dates, not just the mailing date. A statement arriving after the death may concern earlier care. Ask the provider to explain an unfamiliar charge; report suspected misuse if the explanation does not resolve it. Do not create a Medicare account posing as your parent to investigate.

A password is not permission

Your parent’s phone may be in your hand. Their password may be on paper. Neither fact answers whether you are entitled to read their messages or act through an account.

Do not sign in as your parent or reset credentials to make yourself the account holder. Use the provider’s deceased-user process or access expressly authorized for your role.

Find each provider’s help page from its own website. Ask separately about reporting the death, preserving data, obtaining permitted content, memorializing the account and deleting it. Memorializing means retaining a form of the profile after death; the actual features and conditions belong to that provider. It is not the same request as access to private messages.

The provider may require proof of death and legal authority. Apple Support’s August 2026 deceased-account guidance describes verified legal documentation, with requirements varying by country or region. Google’s deceased-user page, checked in 2026, describes reviewed requests, not password release. Neither establishes a procedure for other providers.

Ask the estate lawyer which law applies to a disputed access request where your parent lived. Owning a device and receiving its stored communications can involve different questions. If the account belonged to an employer, contact that employer rather than treating it as a family account.

Hold deletion or memorialization until needed content is preserved or the provider confirms that the change will not prevent its release.

Leave it intact.

Keep the number until you have a reason to release it

The FTC’s two-factor authentication guidance, checked in 2026, explains that verification can involve a text, email, authenticator app or security key. The phone may therefore matter, but it is not the key to every account. Keeping it active does not grant permission to use a code sent to your parent.

Before cancelling the line, ask the carrier how to handle a deceased customer’s service, who may authorize changes, and what will happen to voicemail. Ask the account providers what contact route the authorized person should use. Keep necessary service only through an authorized payment arrangement, following Chapter 7’s recurring-charge test.

Set the next review date around outstanding preservation requests, not an arbitrary number of months. If the line was cancelled, ask the carrier what remains recoverable. Don’t buy a stranger’s promise to retrieve everything.

Keep the handset and any separate memory cards secure. Do not factory-reset it, trade it in or let someone erase it while content questions are outstanding. Do not try to bypass its lock. If you have shared a family plan, ask about the other users’ service before approving a change to the account.

Save the photograph, not every private conversation

Name what matters before asking for access: the porch photograph, the voicemail your parent left you, the recipe sent years ago. A specific request is easier to think through than “save everything.”

Start with copies lawfully yours: messages sent to you or photographs in your own account. For material held only in your parent’s account, request authorized preservation or release. A photograph visible on a screen may not have a separate copy on that device.

When you receive content through permitted access, keep the original files and make a separate backup in storage you control. Open the saved photograph or play the audio to check that it works. A link to an account scheduled for deletion is not a saved file.

Private messages may concern other people too. Keep recovered material private while the authorized person decides what may be shared. Don’t put identity papers or passwords in the family group chat.

The tool: the fraud-prevention week

These seven actions are a work plan, not a waiting period. Move suspected theft or a legal response date ahead of the schedule. Beside each action, write “done on,” the person responsible and the next unanswered question.

  1. Review public details. Ask the obituary publisher about removing sensitive information. Use the actual notice URL on this line. If a service is still ahead, arrange the house sitter privately.
  2. Contact the bureaus. Start with IdentityTheft.gov/CreditBureauContacts. Obtain each company’s deceased-consumer directions, including authority and later review; record a separate result for each.
  3. Route suspicious activity. Identify unfamiliar account activity and contact the verified institution promptly. Use IdentityTheft.gov for suspected identity theft, accurately stating the death and your role. Keep confirmations with the evidence.
  4. Check collection demands. Use the CFPB’s validation and harassment guidance at consumerfinance.gov. Send time-sensitive papers to the authorized representative; complaints and court responses are separate tasks.
  5. Check medical misuse. Review lawfully available service records and report suspected Medicare fraud through Medicare.gov’s fraud page. Note the questioned service date and report reference, not your parent’s full identifiers on this sheet.
  6. Ask before changing digital service. Find the carrier’s and providers’ official deceased-user help pages. Record each URL, permitted requester, preservation question and consequence of closure. Confirm the payment arrangement for anything still needed.
  7. Preserve permitted content. Save what is already yours and request other material through authorized channels. Check each received file and its backup before an approved deletion, cancellation or device handoff.

Write the next unresolved action beside the phone. Then leave the handset where the person responsible can find it, not in the box going to the donation center.

Chapter 11: Your Brother, Your Sister, and a House Full of Things

On the second weekend in June 2016, Kevin stood in our parents’ bedroom with his hand on a chest of drawers neither of us wanted.

Dad had died in March. Mom was still living there. We weren’t emptying her house; we were trying to decide what to do with his things without making her home disappear around her.

Kevin thought the chest should come to me. I thought he wanted it. He wanted something settled before his flight back to Tucson. I wanted to go home.

The top drawer wouldn’t shut properly. Neither of us had room for it.

I asked whether he actually wanted it.

He took his hand off the top. No. He thought I did.

It stayed where it was. We hadn’t even established whose furniture we were discussing.

If you’re in months two and three, you may recognize that room. A cupboard is open, someone has brought packing tape, and a visit has turned into a deadline without anyone agreeing to one.

The return flight is not the deadline

The early weeks gave you appointments. A person told you where to be, what to bring, or which form was missing. Now someone says the house ought to be cleared by Saturday, and Saturday means the day they hired a van.

Ask what actually requires the date. A confirmed tenancy ending, a necessary repair or a lawful sale may need action. Someone’s wish to be finished is different. Record the real requirement and ask the person with authority what must happen by then. You do not have to divide belongings merely because a van is outside.

Permission to enter a house is not permission to allocate its contents. A surviving parent may own the furniture and need the kitchen equipment. Roommates may have belongings there too. Ask before treating everything as something to inherit.

Chapter 4’s freeze rule bought time. This is a discussion method for items the authorized person confirms may be considered, not permission to move them.

Ownership, a will’s instructions and state law come before any family picking system. California Courts’ property-after-death guide, checked in 2026, describes a legal transfer process even when there is a will. Ask your own county probate clerk where to find the official guidance for your state. If ownership or authority is disputed, take the papers to a local estate lawyer before anything leaves.

The legal work of estate administration and distributions belongs to The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide; this chapter stays with the conversation around the belongings.

The work nobody else saw

The child who did the caregiving can hear “we all need an equal say” as though the night calls never happened. The child who lived far away can hear “you weren’t here” as though distance cancelled the relationship.

Do not make a sideboard carry the argument about who visited. If the caregiving needs to be acknowledged, acknowledge it in words. If there is a claim for money spent, route it through the expense record from Chapter 7. Do not silently compensate yourself by taking the sideboard or decide that a sibling’s absence forfeits whatever they may legally receive.

The nearby child has another problem: everybody’s plan requires their hands. “We should get photographs of the dishes” means you should drive there after work, take the photographs, send them and answer the questions about the plates behind the plates.

Name the job.

A distant sibling can organize the pictures, telephone a service provider with permission, or circulate the proposed method. They need an assignment they have accepted, not a general promise to help.

You can say, “I can meet the repair person on Thursday. I cannot spend Sunday packing. Who is taking Sunday?” If nobody agrees, Sunday is unassigned. It is not secretly yours.

A house-clearance deadline may require paid help. Have the authorized person approve the scope, payer and cost before booking it. Don’t assume that being the one who hired the cleaner makes the estate obliged to repay you.

The chipped bowl has two values

An object can be cheap to replace and impossible to replace in your memory.

The chipped mixing bowl is where you remember your mother stirring cake batter. Your sister remembers being told not to touch it. Neither memory comes with a receipt.

Ask what someone wants the object for before arguing about its price. They may want a permitted copy of the recipe or a photograph rather than the bowl. Establish the request.

For a value tally, agree what the figures mean. A dealer’s estimate, an insurance figure and your guess are not interchangeable. If value is uncertain, ask the representative whether a qualified appraisal is needed. Don’t call an item worthless because nobody recognizes it.

And don’t give every story a cash price. You can record that two people want the same object without deciding whose memory costs more.

No choosing while standing in the doorway

Make the preference list away from the house. Use photographs already lawfully taken, with enough detail to tell the brass lamp from the lamp with the bent shade. Give each item an identifier. “The lamp” is not enough when there are lamps in every bedroom.

Send the same version to everyone entitled to participate, rather than just the siblings who answer quickly. Have the authorized person confirm the group; beneficiaries may include other people.
