Let people mark wanted, not wanted or undecided. Set a reasonable reply date everyone has received, with a way to ask for more time. No reply means no reply. It does not mean consent or a lost legal entitlement.

My preferred sentence is this: “I’m not deciding that today. Write it on the list.”

It records a request without approving it, including the promise someone says your father made in a conversation nobody else heard. Record that as a claim, not “belongs to” beside their name.

If a specific gift is already directed by valid papers, that is a question for the authorized person, not a prize in your drawing. If someone disputes those papers, stop the picking discussion about that item. A friendly vote cannot resolve the legal question.

Choose a method before anybody chooses an object. Rotating picks can spread first-choice opportunities; drawing lots can decide an agreed order. A value tally may fit a group that wants to compare estimated amounts. None is a legal formula, and none overrides the will, ownership or other people’s rights.

I prefer a written method to “we’ll be fair.” You can point to the agreement. Otherwise everybody points at themselves.

When the executor is also the daughter

If you are the representative, identify your role. “As your sister, I’d like the quilt. As the representative, I haven’t confirmed that it can be released.”

Keep your preference on the shared page. Don’t exclude it because you are doing the work or hide it because wanting something feels improper. It belongs in the permitted discussion.

Separate practical updates from private information. You can say that an ownership question is outstanding without forwarding identity documents, confidential advice or account numbers to the family chat. Ask your lawyer what information you may share when you’re unsure.

If you propose paying for packing or storage, record the quoted amount, what it covers and who would pay. Keep an expense out of the preference tally. Spending money to pack an object does not make that object yours.

You cannot promise that everyone will like the answer. You can tell them what question remains, who is answering it and when you expect the next update. If the date slips, say why rather than letting silence carry the message.

When your sibling has the appointment

If someone else is the representative, send a focused written request. Ask for the current list of belongings being considered, the proposed method and the next update date. Identify the item that matters to you and any ownership information you actually have.

“I’d like to be included when you discuss the sewing machine. Please tell me whether it’s available to consider, and when you’ll send the preference list” is clearer than a chain of messages about why nobody tells you anything.

Propose an update rhythm that fits the work. A weekly email can be useful during an active clearing period; a later date may make more sense while an answer is outstanding. These are suggested arrangements, not a legal reporting schedule. Ask for urgent changes promptly rather than waiting for the agreed email.

Legal reporting rights depend on your role and state law. This list cannot replace required estate records. If requests go unanswered or you suspect unauthorized removals, preserve your messages and ask an estate lawyer about options and response dates. Don’t take something yourself to settle it.

If the disagreement is about preferences rather than rights, you can ask whether a neutral mediator would help. Confirm the fee and what the mediation would cover. Do not use a meeting to pressure someone into giving up a legal claim they don’t understand.

No method requires you to sit in a room where you are threatened. Leave an unsafe meeting. Use written communication or professional help instead of treating physical attendance as proof that you care about the family.

The tool: the dividing method

This is a proposed agreement about preferences, not a transfer document. Put it on one dated page, attached to the shared item list. Everything material goes in writing; an oral change does not quietly replace the page.

  1. Confirm the boundary. The authorized person identifies which items can enter the discussion, who may participate and what questions remain. Exclude another owner’s property, legally directed gifts and disputed items until cleared. Mark every preference as provisional; nothing on this page authorizes removal.
  2. Collect requests. Circulate identified photographs and one common list. Each participant marks their preferences by an agreed date. Record missing replies and arrange follow-up rather than treating silence as assent. Keep disputed promises visible as unresolved claims.
  3. Agree on the choosing rule. Record the method, order, treatment of ties and how a pass works before picks begin. For rotating picks, write how the first chooser changes between rounds. Put anything requiring valuation or legal advice on hold instead of improvising an exception.
  4. Record and check the result. Write each proposed recipient beside the item identifier, including holds and things nobody wants. Circulate the result for written confirmation. The authorized person checks that any eventual release is lawful and permitted; record an approved handoff separately. A disagreement stops that item, not a rush to the car.

For a worked example, suppose two participants are confirmed as eligible to express preferences about a small set of permitted household items. Both want a mixing bowl and neither wants a bedside cabinet. One also wants a framed print; the other wants a mantel clock. All requests are provisional.

They draw lots for the first pick, agreeing to reverse the starting order next round. The first chooser provisionally selects the bowl. The other selects the clock, then starts the next round and passes. The first chooser selects the print. Nobody wants the cabinet; it stays unchosen, not assigned to make the count look even.

Before a handoff, the representative finds that the bowl may belong to the surviving parent. That selection goes on hold, and the parent is asked. The drawing did not answer the ownership question. A packed box does not answer it either.

The example assumes no conflicting gift, value question or other restriction. It cannot calculate inheritance shares or establish what the estate can release.

Keep the page. Date corrections, obtain participants’ written agreement and get the authorized person’s check where necessary.

The cereal aisle is not on the schedule

You can get through a morning of papers and then stand in front of a box of cereal unable to remember what you came to buy. Something on the shelf looks like the breakfast your father ate. Or nothing particular happened, and you cannot keep shopping.

It can happen early or much later. There is no week when it is supposed to arrive.

The National Cancer Institute’s patient summary on grief, updated in February 2025 and checked again in 2026, describes sudden pangs prompted by reminders or no apparent cause. It also says people’s grief responses differ. That is more useful than a timetable telling you where you ought to be by now.

Don’t use your ability to complete a form as evidence that you aren’t grieving, or your brother’s quieter face as evidence that he isn’t. You can ask for help without comparing how visibly each of you hurts.

Make the help small enough to accept. Ask someone to bring supper, accompany you to an appointment or take over a permitted task with a specific end. If you cannot bear another question about how you feel, say that you’d like company without questions tonight.

Help that does not start with another packing box

For older adults and their families, the Administration for Community Living’s Eldercare Locator connects people to local services at eldercare.acl.gov. Its contact number, checked in 2026, is 1-800-677-1116. The CFPB’s September 2026 guidance specifically names it for older Americans and caregivers, including free legal aid for eligible older adults. Ask which local service fits the living person who needs help. It is not a promise of free representation for every adult child or every estate dispute.

Chapter 8 mentioned VA bereavement counseling. The Department of Veterans Affairs’ September 2026 page identifies possible surviving spouse, child or parent eligibility. It covers service members dying while serving the country and Reservists or National Guard members dying on active duty. It also names Veterans receiving Vet Center services at death and Veterans or service members who died by suicide.

This is narrower than “my parent was a Veteran.” Ask the nearest Vet Center about your circumstances. VA lists free outreach, counseling and referrals, with in-person and telehealth options; its 2026 page gives 1-877-927-8387 (TTY 711) for contact. You do not have to solve the eligibility question before making the call.

Call your doctor or a mental health professional promptly if you cannot cope, sleep or eat adequately, or distress is keeping you from basic daily tasks. Especially if this has been continuing for weeks, don’t dismiss it as something you must endure until the estate is finished. Tell the clinician what has changed and how long it has been happening so they can assess what help you need.

The National Institute of Mental Health’s guidance checked in 2026 recommends professional help when symptoms interfere with daily life or you are struggling to cope. Numbness alone is not a diagnosis. You can still ask for help.

For thoughts of suicide or urges to harm yourself, get immediate help. NIMH’s crisis guidance checked in 2026 directs people to call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and to call 911 in a life-threatening emergency. Tell someone you trust what is happening. The belongings can wait.

When nobody needs a form tonight

As the work thins, an evening can feel worse because nothing tells you what to do with it. You had a reason to sit at the table for weeks. Tonight the next letter has not arrived.

You don’t have to start clearing another cupboard to earn the right to sit down. You can leave tomorrow’s job on the page and telephone someone without making the call about the house.

Send the preference list before the next visit. Put an agreed stopping time in the message. When that time comes, close the cupboard and go home without settling the last object.

Chapter 12: Day 90, and the Help Worth Paying For

Near day ninety after my mother died in 2019, Sam slid my notebook back across the desk and asked which question I wanted answered first.

I had booked a ninety-minute consultation with the Chillicothe estate lawyer. The folder’s elastic strap left a dent in the paper. My first question was “Am I finished?”

He asked what was still outstanding. I turned pages. There was a tax-return question, an unanswered letter, and a note that said “check this” without saying what this was.

I left with jobs assigned and a question for the tax preparer. I paid for a list of decisions I no longer had to guess at.

If you are approaching day ninety, put your notebook on the table. Some entries may be finished. Others may have started only when a new envelope arrived. The final income tax return can reach into the following April. That is work to schedule, not evidence that the first three months went wrong.

If funds are insufficient or personal responsibility is uncertain, get tax and legal advice before committing money; do not ignore the filing or payment date while that question is answered.

For final-return, refund, transcript, and estate-tax work, see The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide.

Pay for the question you cannot safely answer

Choose someone who prepares deceased taxpayers’ final returns. An enrolled agent or CPA with relevant experience may be appropriate, as may another qualified preparer whose work fits the return. If there is a trust, rental business or other business interest, say that when making the appointment. Ask whether the person handles that kind of work or will refer it elsewhere.

The IRS’s “Choosing a tax professional” page, updated in August 2026, describes differing credentials and levels of expertise and links its preparer directory. A preparer tax identification number permits paid preparation; it does not prove experience with your parent’s situation. Check claimed credentials with the issuing body and ask about the actual task.

An estate attorney answers a different set of questions. A disputed will, uncertain ownership of jointly held property, insufficient assets to meet debts, or real estate in another state warrants legal assessment. A blended family may need help establishing rights even when everyone is being civil. Tell the lawyer the facts that complicate the answer, rather than asking for “some paperwork help.”

Use Chapter 11’s state-check route for local guidance. Ask a lawyer licensed in the relevant state whether another state’s counsel is needed.

A financial adviser is for a decision about managing money that belongs to you, not a substitute for sorting your parent’s returns or establishing ownership. Broader investment choices can wait until the money, taxes and immediate needs are understood. A deadline affecting an inherited account cannot wait merely because you are postponing investment shopping; flag it to the preparer and account custodian promptly.

My rule is to choose the adviser yourself, not appoint the stranger who contacted you after the death. That is a precaution, not a finding that every unsolicited offer is fraudulent. The SEC’s Investor.gov site, checked in 2026, links a “Check Out Your Investment Professional” resource and warns about pressure to act now. Begin there to check the person’s claimed registration, and ask how they are paid before discussing a product.

A small engagement needs a clear edge

“Review these papers and identify deadlines needing action” defines a task. “Take care of everything” leaves the scope uncertain.

You can request a flat fee for a limited consultation or return, but the professional may use another billing method. Get the scope, rate, likely additional charges and payer in writing before agreeing. Ask what changes would require another approval. Do not assume the estate will reimburse a consultation you hire personally.

At the first meeting, identify the client. The lawyer may represent the estate’s representative rather than every beneficiary. Ask what information can be shared and whether someone with a separate interest needs independent advice. Paying part of a bill does not resolve those questions.

Bring the focused question page and the Chapter 6 inventory, plus the papers the office requests. Ask which original documents are needed and keep a record of anything the office retains. Use the secure delivery method it identifies for tax records and identity information.

Ask what sorting or authorized document requests you can do yourself. Sorting by tax year is different from deciding how an amount should be taxed. Leave that judgment to the preparer.

Before you leave, establish the next deliverable and who is responsible for it. A consultation may give advice without including the filing of any form. A prepared return may still await review and the proper signature. Write those distinctions beside the appointment entry.

When the right office cannot take you

“Our next appointment is in May” doesn’t answer the date on the notice beside your phone, so read that date to the intake person before accepting a place on the calendar that may be too late. Ask whether someone there can assess the time-sensitive question sooner or suggest an appropriate referral. If the office cannot help in time, keep looking through the verified professional and referral routes above. An appointment isn’t protection.

Suppose you have a letter you don’t understand and quotes from two offices. One offers a short meeting next week. The other offers a larger package next month. Compare them against what the letter requires, not just the bottom-line price. Ask the first office whether its meeting can address that letter and the second whether its proposed work includes an assessment soon enough to help you act before the date you read over the phone. The cheaper quote may leave that job undone.

You needn’t tell your parent’s whole history to every receptionist. Give the relevant state, your actual role, the kind of problem and the date on the paper; if the office needs to see the notice before deciding whether it can help, ask how to send it safely.

Check later availability. The IRS’s Topic 254, updated in September 2026, recommends considering whether a preparer will remain available to answer questions after filing. At intake, ask how later questions are handled and whether that work costs extra. Don’t assume “we prepared it” includes help with every subsequent letter.

If the professional cannot continue, ask who, if anyone, has agreed to take over. Arrange access to the work already done and verify the replacement’s role. A referral name is a lead; it isn’t confirmation that the new person has your papers or knows about the approaching date.

Make the appointment usable

Tell the office what would let you participate. You may need a telephone appointment because you live out of state, a quieter room because hearing is difficult, or time to read a written explanation. Ask what it can arrange and what that would cost. Don’t nod through advice you cannot hear because everyone else seems ready to finish.

If another person comes with you, establish whether they are there to take notes or participate in the decisions, and ask the professional what permission is needed before the companion sits down with the open file. They can write while you listen. That doesn’t mean speaking for you or receiving every private paper afterward.

Try saying it back. “I understand you’re reviewing the letter, but you haven’t agreed to send a response.” Let the professional correct your understanding. If the answer depends on information you haven’t supplied, ask which information. Keep that uncertainty visible instead of leaving with a confident instruction nobody actually gave.

Pressure is not a qualification

An actual response deadline deserves prompt action. A sales pitch demanding a signature tonight deserves verification. Ask for the notice or official source establishing the date, and contact the known professional independently.

The IRS’s September 2026 Topic 254 warns against preparers whose fees depend on a percentage of the refund or who propose putting the refund into their own accounts. It tells you never to sign a blank form.

Use Chapter 9’s finder check for recovery offers. Decline an engagement if fees remain unexplained in writing or you are pressured to grant authority you don’t understand.

If the budget is tight, the IRS’s Topic 254 names VITA and Tax Counseling for the Elderly as possible free preparation routes for qualifying taxpayers. Ask the local site whether it can handle this final individual return and your signing circumstances. The IRS says an out-of-scope return is referred for paid help; eligibility does not mean every estate-related task is covered.

The tool: the day-90 review

Make one dated review page with four fields for each open item. They can run across a sheet or underneath each other in your notebook. This is an audit of unanswered work, not a demand to finish it all today.

  1. Open item. Name the unresolved question precisely: a missing tax-year statement, an unconfirmed claim submission, or a disputed invoice. Refer to the existing file instead of recopying sensitive account details.
  2. Who owes the answer. Name the person or office expected to respond and the person responsible for following up. If a professional has not accepted the work, record that; an appointment request does not assign the job.
  3. Deadline and source. Enter the full date, applicable tax year or claim, official source or notice, and date checked. Bring over the SSA lump-sum date and the applicable VA claim dates or confirmed exceptions from Chapter 8’s sheet, including any intent-to-file completion date. A blank needs prompt verification.
  4. Next action with a date. Write the call, document request or authorized filing needed, who will do it, and when. Distinguish a follow-up reminder from the legal deadline. Attach submission proof when the action is completed.

For example, “final return” is too broad. “Preparer to confirm whether a missing interest statement includes amounts paid after death” gives the next call a purpose. The deadline field holds the confirmed filing and payment dates, or says they still need immediate verification. The next-action field names who will request the statement and the day they will contact the office.

Bring other unresolved entries forward by reference. Check for new agency requests, not just the questions already on your page.

The box is not ready for the shredder

Chapter 6 promised a records check here. Do not destroy papers because the ninety days are over.

The IRS’s “How long should I keep records?” page, reviewed in June 2026, ties tax-supporting records to the applicable return’s limitation period. It treats property records separately, linking their retention to the year of disposal, and warns that other purposes may require longer retention. That is why I will not give your whole box one discard date.

Add a records section to the review sheet. For each record type, write “keep until,” the date or condition given, who supplied it and where the records will be stored. Ask the representative, tax preparer and estate lawyer which papers support returns, property basis, claims and court filings. Basis is the tax value used when calculating a gain or loss; preserve the supporting papers without calculating it from this chapter.

Put filed returns and their supporting records on a line. Give property and valuation papers their own line, separate from payment receipts. Include claim correspondence and legal originals rather than assuming the tax preparer’s answer covers everything. Record the latest applicable instruction. If the answer depends on a future event, write the condition and a review date, not an invented expiration date.

Ask what must remain on paper; scanning does not settle that. Use Chapter 10’s preservation check for authorized digital records and identify their custodian.

Keep pending records.

If professional answers conflict, or a claim is unresolved, leave the record in place while you obtain clarification. An approaching retention date prompts another check; it does not override a later need.

Pick the earliest unanswered deadline on the review page. Contact the office responsible for that answer, with the relevant paper beside the phone. When the call is recorded, put the folder somewhere you can find it tomorrow. The table can be used for supper tonight.

The Green Folder in the Second Drawer

A year after our own papers were signed, in May 2025, Jess sat at my kitchen table with a stack of school papers and the green folder beside her elbow.

She had come down from Columbus for the afternoon. The papers had red marks on them. Mine had tabs. We pushed both piles away from the patch of sunlight coming through the window because she wanted to put her tea there.

“Is this still where you keep it?” she asked.

The second drawer, under the silverware. Yes.

She looked toward the drawer, then back at me. I realized she was checking the distance between an answer and a place she could actually find. I had been treating the folder as something I maintained. She was treating it as something she might someday have to reach for without asking me.

I stopped explaining how much work it had been.

What those ninety days changed

By then I had buried both parents and spent enough afternoons sorting their papers to know how much affection can coexist with irritation. I could miss my mother while wishing she had put a name on an envelope. Neither feeling cancelled the other. That irritation is most of why the folder in my own second drawer exists now; building it is its own job, and Estate Planning for Beginners is where that job gets done, not here.

What changed in me wasn’t a filing system. It was smaller habits, worn in by ninety days of practice. I write the call down now — who I spoke to, what they said, the date — instead of trusting I’ll remember it by supper. I ask an institution whether it needs a certified copy and whether it returns it before I order a single one, rather than guessing a number and hoping it’s enough. I check whose debt a bill actually is before I reach for a checkbook; most of the time, if it isn’t mine and it isn’t the estate’s, it stays unpaid. And I open the mail. All of it, the day it arrives, even the envelopes I’d rather leave on the counter.

Sitting across from my daughter, I wanted another afternoon exactly like that one, and then another. I couldn’t give her a reason to need those habits less. I could only tell her where one drawer was, and let that be enough for one Tuesday.

She didn’t promise me that she would handle everything. I didn’t ask her to.

Everything includes jobs you haven’t named and days the other person has already promised to their own family. I could tell Jess where my papers lived without trying to claim those days in advance.

You don’t have to keep being the emergency person

For the first weeks after a death, being reachable can become the shape of your whole day. You bring the phone into the bathroom. You leave a meal unfinished when it rings. You start answering an ordinary question as if a stranger at a counter is waiting for the correct words.

If that has become your habit, notice it before deciding it is your permanent job.

Someone may still need an answer about your parent’s affairs. The open work on Chapter 12’s review page remains real. A reply date does not disappear because you want a quiet evening. But being responsible for a named task is different from remaining available to everyone, for anything, indefinitely.

I had learned that feeling frightened of a bill didn’t tell me whose bill it was. A fresh envelope could still contain news I hadn’t known to look for. Neither was a reason to surrender my entire evening before I had read the page.

Put one name and one reply date beside the open item, so you know who’s answering it and when. Then tell a relative, plainly, that tonight’s call cannot be another discussion about the house. If you need someone to take over an authorized task, ask them and confirm that they have accepted it. Don’t substitute silence for a handoff.

I dislike advice that tells a tired person to find a grand new purpose. Some days I wanted to finish an errand without someone needing a document.

You may want an evening in which your parent’s name is not followed by an account number. You may also want to say that name over supper. Someone willing to listen can hear about your father without helping with a form.

And you needn’t make all the conversation tender. An argument, a bad habit, a visit you disliked — those belong to the memory too. This book has asked you to handle tasks carefully; it has not asked you to revise your parent into someone easier to miss.

If the relationship was painful, completing the practical work does not oblige you to announce forgiveness. Leave that question unanswered if it isn’t answered yet. A signed receipt or a returned key cannot settle it for you.

For me, grief sometimes occupied a whole evening and sometimes appeared in a sentence I had nearly spoken. I would start to tell my mother something and remember that there was no call to make. On another day I could go from breakfast to bedtime without that interruption, then feel unsettled when I noticed. I didn’t learn anything useful from the contrast. I missed her. I went to bed.

If distress is making daily life hard or is worsening, tell your doctor or a mental health professional what is happening so they can assess the help you need. The National Institute of Mental Health’s help guidance, checked in 2026, names difficulty completing daily tasks as a reason for professional help. Chapter 11 has the detailed help routes; you need not wait until the remaining papers are dealt with to use them.

Something with your own name on it

When you’re ready to put this book down, the next task may still concern your parent. Or it may concern you.

If the work now needs court authority or continued estate administration, follow that question into The Executor’s Step-by-Step Guide with your own court’s current instructions and legal advice beside it.

If you are looking at your own unmarked envelopes and wondering what another person would make of them, Estate Planning for Beginners takes up that separate work.

Read what fits your question, rather than borrowing a new worry from a book title. The unresolved date on your review page deserves attention; an optional reading plan does not deserve the same urgency.

Choose something, too, that has nothing to do with papers. Keep the dental appointment you postponed. Ask a friend to meet you for lunch without bringing the folder. Walk down a street that isn’t on the way to your parent’s house. These aren’t treatments or proof of recovery. They are things you are allowed to want.

If today was the funeral, this afternoon at my table may seem a long way off. You do not have to imagine yourself there. Stay with the work that belongs to today. There is no duty to turn what has happened into a useful experience before you have slept.

If it has been months, you don’t owe anyone a performance of being finished. An unanswered letter and a reasonably good day can exist together.

At the table, Jess lifted her school papers off the folder. She had marked a page while I was talking. The tea was cold. I had not told her everything I might want to tell her about my parents, or about being the person who answered the phone afterward.

I could tell her another time. I could also ask about her day.

Before supper, I asked her to put the folder away herself. I wanted to see whether my description matched the kitchen she could see.

She opened the drawer beneath the spoons and found the space. The folder went in without moving anything else. She shut the drawer with her hand, and I turned back to the stove.
